title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
📚 Just finished reading Elon Musk's biography by @WalterIsaacson (beware ~720 pages).
What a story...I learned a ton and I seriously need to recalibrate myself going forward. 😅
It's one of those books that changes your brain chemistry. Highly recommend the book.
I really love "the algorithm" he's using in all of his companies (excerpt from the book):
"1. Question every requirement. Each should come with the name of the person who made it. You should never accept that a requirement came from a department, such as from “the legal department” or “the safety department.” You need to know the name of the real person who made that requirement. Then you should question it, no matter how smart that person is. Requirements from smart people are the most dangerous, because people are less likely to question them. Always do so, even if the requirement came from me. Then make the requirements less dumb.
2. Delete any part or process you can. You may have to add them back later. In fact, if you do not end up adding back at least 10% of them, then you didn’t delete enough.
3. Simplify and optimize. This should come after step two. A common mistake is to simplify and optimize a part or a process that should not exist.
4. Accelerate cycle time. Every process can be speeded up. But only do this after you have followed the first three steps. In the Tesla factory, I mistakenly spent a lot of time accelerating processes that I later realized should have been deleted.
5. Automate. That comes last. The big mistake in Nevada and at Fremont was that I began by trying to automate every step. We should have waited until all the requirements had been questioned, parts and processes deleted, and the bugs were shaken out.
Corollaries:
* All technical managers must have hands-on experience. For example, managers of software teams must spend at least 20% of their time coding. Solar roof managers must spend time on the roofs doing installations. Otherwise, they are like a cavalry leader who can’t ride a horse or a general who can’t use a sword.
* Comradery is dangerous. It makes it hard for people to challenge each other’s work. There is a tendency to not want to throw a colleague under the bus. That needs to be avoided.
* It’s OK to be wrong. Just don’t be confident and wrong.
* Never ask your troops to do something you’re not willing to do.
* Whenever there are problems to solve, don’t just meet with your managers. Do a skip level, where you meet with the level right below your managers.
* When hiring, look for people with the right attitude. Skills can be taught. Attitude changes require a brain transplant.
* A maniacal sense of urgency is our operating principle.
* The only rules are the ones dictated by the laws of physics. Everything else is a recommendation."
---
I also love his concept of a “surge” where he set an unrealistic expectations to “extrude shit out of the system”.
It's also crazy just how much risk he was willing to take upon himself.
Obviously don't agree with every single thing he's proposing but his first principles thinking and low risk aversion is something all of us could learn from.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
🥳 Challenge completed!!! - 30 days of non-stop (~10 hour on avg) live streaming my coding and work on the Open-NLLB machine translation project! (allows translation between 200+ human languages).
A bit more about the project:
After OpenAI's ChatGPT was released the whole world got caught up in the AI frenzy (and for a good reason). While systems such as Meta's Llama and OpenAI's GPT-4 are incredibly powerful - they only focus on English language.
Similarly, for machine translation systems, Meta released a powerful NLLB ("no language left behind") MT system that supports 202 languages - but they didn't release open-source checkpoints (they were released under non-commercial CC-NC-BY 4.0 license).
The main goal of this effort is to release truly open-source NLLB checkpoints that can be freely used even for commercial purposes.
The extended goal of this project is to scale up beyond the original 3.3B parameters dense transformers (7B+) and also support non-English LLMs.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Here are the AI news that marked previous week! 🧠 (brace yourselves it's been a crazy period - I don't say that lightly)
* Super cool paper (congrats @_rockt, @chrisantha_f & team): "PromptBreeder: Self-Referential Self-Improvement via Prompt Evolution"
At this point we all know of these clever LLM prompts - "Let's think step by step" being arguably the most famous one.
The thing is such hand-crafted prompts are obviously sub-optimal. In this paper LLMs evolve their own prompts through self-referential self-improvement. Reminds me of @kenneth0stanley's Picbreeder work (I suppose the paper title was inspired by it :) ).
* 21 year old CS student (@LukeFarritor) made a major breakthrough in @natfriedman's Vesuvius challenge and won 40.000$: his ML algo read the first word from an unopened Herculaneum scroll! The word is apparently "πορφυρας" which means "purple dye" or "cloths of purple".
The scrolls were discovered in 1750s but are in such a state that they can not be opened and we must use ML to figure out what's written on them.
Blog:
* @chipro's new blog post is out: Multimodality and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs):
Nice high level overview of the topic! I would just add multilinguality to the LLM research directions :)) (see my project as well:
* @nathanbenaich just released this year's state of AI report!
Check it out:
It's probably the best high level resource to figure out what happened over the last year - thus making it perfect for people who are not in the "AI trenches" like myself, but I'm sure I've missed out on important details myself as well :))
* Amazing new paper introducing RingAttention (nice work @haoliuhl!), enabling scaling context lengths to 0.5M tokens and beyond! Well kind of, depends on device count - more precisely it enables training and inference of sequences that are up to device count times longer than previously possible:
Related work, introduces StreamingLLMs (allowing for infinite context lengths? I wonder what are the caveats, it's not exact attn mechanism it uses sparse attn pattern):
* Reading someone's thoughts? Sounds like sci-fi? It's not, check out @iScienceLuvr's new paper:
we just had him in my Discord server as well (will try to upload the vid soon!).
* Open source alternative to GPT-4 vision: LLaVA (Large Language and Vision Assistant): and related cool paper "Improved baselines with Visual Instruction Tuning" that further improves LLaVA:
* People are pushing the state of the art by fine-tuning open source LLM base models like recent Mistral 7B model, check out this:
* Related, Mistral AI has published their paper: (9 pages only)
* @OpenAI's DALLE-3 paper is out as well:
* Hyped up new paper "Language Models Represent Space and Time": They show they can find an actual wold map inside of Llama 2 activations. There's been a debate on their definition of a "world model" as commonly defined. Just by showing that the model has an internal representation of a world MAP doesn't mean it has the model of the world.
* @Replit is giving out free access to their AIs! (code completion and code assistance) They'll be burning a ton of GPUs but this might be a great opportunity for beginners to check them out: they are a "cloud based IDE" but on steroids if you never heard of them.
* This is big! OpenWebMath, a massive dataset containing every math document found on the internet (14.7B tokens) - with equations in LaTeX format. We've shown that datasets like these improve reasoning of LLMs and datasets contributions are among the most important contributions in the field.
Paper: (@keirp1 et al)
* "Everything about Distributed Training and Efficient Finetuning" - in depth blog, highly recommend if interested in this topic.
Phew. :)) Accelerate. 🫡
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F8UzOXdWkAAASOj.jpg
Quoting @_lewtun
Here's a simple recipe to train a 7B model that outperforms Llama2 70B on MT Bench 🥇
1. SFT Mistral 7B on the UltraChat dataset
2. Align the SFT model to the UltraFeedback dataset with "direct preference optimisation" (DPO)

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
some thoughts on the "doing good better" book by @willmacaskill (effective altruism co-founder)
in general I liked the book, ton of interesting ideas, and it gave me some mental models that I can "hang on top of my existing lattice" of mental models and think better
i love the fusion of concepts from economy and moral philosophy, it's clear that it opens one up for attacks but i think it's brave and smart
on the other hand i feel that book missed out on the opportunity to push this EA idea to its extreme :))
why not create QALY/WALY markets?
EA funds sponsored by rich individuals/universities/etc who want to maximize their good-doing?
why not let the EA fund manager get some proper fee (minding the incentives) and maximize the good as a professional do-gooder? :)
this is a semi-joke - but there might be something in this idea...
at times the reasoning in the book seems way off and oversimplifications of the real world are pushed too far
i feel it's partly due to munger's "reason-respecting tendency" aka a psychological tendency that increases the confidence of the conclusion even when the explanation is utterly false
e.g. the reasoning that went into the calculation behind whether Laura (Oxford PhD) should enter politics is borderline dangerous
it missed out on 2nd / higher order effects, e.g. it didn't account for the fact that she might inadvertently do bad things as a) we're not perfectly rational agents and b) we live in a game-theoretically incomplete information world
so having an arbitrary number at the end and using that as an excuse to make a decision felt wrong in this example (despite the attempts of being "conservative" and using lower bounds, it lacked a more robust risks analysis)
similarly in the heart attack example, excerpt:
"Now suppose there had been a paramedic around when the woman collapsed. This paramedic would have surely restarted her heart without causing injury, but, while I was running toward the woman, I pushed the paramedic out of the way and started performing CPR myself. In this case, I still saved her life, but if I hadn’t, the paramedic would have been able to do the same thing without causing damage. In this case, how should I feel about my actions? Am I a hero? After all, I “saved a life!”Of course I’m not a hero. The good I do is not a matter of the direct benefits I cause. Rather, it is the difference I make. Even though I technically saved this woman’s life, I actually did harm overall"
phew
if we're playing the "yeah but what if" game let's push it a bit further
what about 2nd and higher order effects?
imagine this was not a woman but a man
imagine this was Munich back in 1931 and you saved this man's life...
you get the point...
Here is one more example (excerpt from the book):
"we found that a 10 percent increase in the fraction of immigrants in the population reduces native wages by about 1 percent, and found no evidence of significant reductions in native employment"
this feels like that fellow who drowned in a river that averaged only 18 inches deep
using statistics incorrectly is more dangerous than not using any quantitative measure in the first place as it gives the impression of authority and thus exploits yet another human psychological tendency increasing the believability of the statement
one last comment regarding the "earning to give" approach:
i feel the book overemphasizes the greedy strategy (in the computer science sense of the word)
if you invest in markets instead and then only later in life you give back (a la buffet, gates et al) that might be much more effective than taking a portion of your earnings to invest into charities (seems like that's william's favorite strategy)
that's a wrap, just some thoughts & ideas I thought might be worth sharing :) if you read it all the way to the very end congrats :)
happy to hear your counter-arguments
as @Plinz says, the reason i share ideas is to submit them for a peer review

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] Some things I wish I knew earlier in my career:
* When applying for a job - always negotiate. Be it Microsoft, DeepMind, or your local startup / whatever company. Companies will always try to save money on you (unless you're a superstar & you understand this dynamics). In retrospect I could have done a much better job but I was afraid that if I negotiated my terms I would have lost the offer. I esp. felt like that for DeepMind - who am I to miss this opportunity, just accept whatever you get. In retrospect I was stupid, but I didn't know any better back then.
If you're outside of the tech hubs, you're likely to get a MUCH worse offer at big tech. THEY WILL NOT TELL YOU THIS. E.g. in Serbia, they didn't offer us sign-up stocks at all, the offer in retrospect was terrible. Also it's hard to immediately become an FTE and so most people are initially "out-sourced" to Microsoft, you're a "contractor". So even though you're effectively in Microsoft in those early days you're legally not and thus your comp is terrible.
The worst thing is when applying for DeepMind I already knew I should negotiate but I was afraid I would lose the offer.
When I was applying for Microsoft in Serbia I got a salary that looked amazing but now that I have a much broader perspective I would have immediately left for the USA. SF in particular (now the situation is a bit worse).
* If seeking high salaries go to SF (counting in the costs of living). London's comp is terrible compared to the USA (again unless you're a superstar). Or fight for USA salary whereever you work. I have friends in Serbia who live like kings because they have SF salary and 10% the cost of living...
* You likely still don't realize just how hard working some people are. If you're not obsessed with what you do, you DO NOT have a chance of becoming the best at anything. Low hanging fruit does not exist. Hard, smart, obsessed work. If it's worth a while many people are competing for it. Additionally a percentage of your competition will be neurodivergent (e.g. Asperger's) so it's much easier for them. They are naturally obsessed they don't have the breadth of curiosity.
That leads me to the next point.
* Deeply internalize the concept of the opportunity cost: yes you can do X but if you say yes to X you're saying no to infinite other number of paths. I spent too many years learning languages, pushing my body to the extreme, and doing a ton of different things (including traveling to over 33 countries, etc.). I'm not saying it's bad, it's ultimately the exploration/exploitation trade off, but be careful in your exploration. While you're exploring some guy/gal out there, e.g. Mr Beast, is doing one thing obsessively since he/she was 13 (or younger). You barely stand a chance. There are exceptions.
I don't have the time nowadays to practice my lang skills (unless I make it a part of daily life by surrounding myself with people who speak those langs) - so skill naturally deteriorates. Did it pay off?
You only have so many years in your life, and your decisions in the early part of your career are disproportionately important. Same as with investing. The compounding effect is a fact of life. And it's everywhere. And powerlaw is everywhere.
* Big tech doesn't have a monopoly on talent: you're equally likely to find the best people in the world in the best startups. And you're almost surely going to find more passionate people in startups. Most big tech jobs are, wait for it, super boring. Just because someone has "Google" in their profile description doesn't mean they're working on fun stuff. Imagine how many ultra boring tech components need to be maintained across Chrome, Android, even when working on ML projects. They're probably learning less than you are also.
Just a random brain dump, have a ton more to say.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
the issue with the current AI regulation / doom debate is the fact that:
* philosophers like yudkowsky are not sufficiently familiar with the technology/research, how it works, and don't spend enough time probing these systems to stay grounded and realistic about the capabilities. they're not the builders of this technology.
* ML engs/researchers who know just the right hyperparams for the next billion $ run often don't spend enough time playing at the prompt level and getting that visceral understanding of what the existing systems can already do (if you just nicely ask them to do it :)). they also mostly lack broader understanding of philosophical/societal questions.
* The prompt-masters & the fine-tuners of existing god-like artifacts (many of whom entered the field in the last year or so) mostly don't have an understanding of ai research (and again same for the philosophical/societal components...)
i.e. it seems to me that there are important dimensions of knowledge at play here that are surprisingly decorrelated:
* knowledge of hardcore ai research
* knowledge of what these systems can do in practical applications (think goodside etc. who spend all of their time just prompting these systems, "driving the car" vs "car builder" analogy is mostly correct)
* broader knowledge of policies, societal & philosophical (ethics, moral philosophy, etc.) background
being cognizant of the above, the right answer is to keep the debate open, keep exchange ideas, stay humble, and prevent preemptive overregulation (which already seems to be way on way)
one more dangerous tendency I've observed is to take the "ai godfathers"' words as the ground truth
first of all just because they had a tremendous impact over the years doesn't mean they are the best at this moment of time (as the matter of fact they're not)
best ai research ideas likely won't come from hinton but from a 25 year old somewhere in the world
same goes for best prompting techniques etc.
be aware of the halo effect as well, just because someone is top expert at X doesn't automatically transfer to topic Y
shower thoughts, certainly lot of room for attacks, don't have time to overpolish

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
I solved one of Chollet's ARC tasks with GPT-4 V (well, almost :)). let me walk you through what I've done.
it's just a matter of time when the vision part of the GPT-4 V is good enough at spatial reasoning / localization (current prod model doesn't even try to address this) before we can solve the ARC challenge completely.
it can then be reduced to a simple next token prediction + some tool use (codegen + access to an interpreter) to circumvent tokenizer issues (or just fix tokenization in the first place).
here is the final conversation that I had where GPT-4 successfully solved the challenge I gave it:
but let me walk you through the process a bit and how I thought about this.
i first realized that a good representation will be crucial here so i tried to prompt the model to reason a bit better by spelling out the image in terms of letters.
(note: P stands for purple, C - cyan, B - blue, G - gray, R - red, Y - yellow, O - orange, X - black/placeholder that you need to solve for)
so I gave it the image, spelled the first row out:
1 -> PCCBCGBGCRRBBRRCGBGCBCCP
and told it to spell the rest out, not to use any code generation but simply analyze the image and generate the response.
i immediately realized the localization is still not built-in. first the model realized itself that this will be impossible (self-awareness? kek):
"Upon further consideration, I realize that manually analyzing and spelling out the color patterns for each of the 23 remaining rows without error and within a reasonable timeframe would not be feasible. This task would normally be performed algorithmically, given the complexity and the potential for human error in such a repetitive and detailed task.
If you need assistance with writing such a script or have any other questions or tasks that I can assist you with, please let me know!"
then with some further manipulation I got it to spell out only the 2nd row - it failed spectacularly (as I expected).
next up I decided to circumvent the need to use the image capability all-together and help the model by spelling out the colors myself (I believe this is the easier part of solving this particular task).
is the reasoning good enough? can do model notice vertical/horizontal symmetry and just leverage its next token prediction?
unfortunately the model failed, I suspect 2 reasons for that:
* tokenization issues (even mirroring the string is hard, I know there are some fixes for this but I don't remember which one feel free to comment below!)
* counting (it gave many more letters for each of the rows instead just 6)
here is that failed attempt:
finally using code-gen with a minor feedback (hint: leverage symmetry) the model managed to solve the task.
---
ok, after having written all of this I realize there is a lot of room for improving these systems.
but the good thing is: I don't see any fundamental limitation with this whole approach:
* image -> "color letter representation" can already be solved with existing research + some good engineering
* representation -> solution as well, if the model does a bit of self-reflection this looks doable.
next 5 years will be just wild.
people don't understand that historical analogies don't do it justice.
congrats @TheRealRPuri & team.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F--eAudWQAAl9Fk.png

similarly once you start operating at a scale you realize how many libs were not designed for it
i'm constantly hitting 1 TB RAM limit, i'm constantly struggling with bloated memory (e.g. huggingface turns my dataset from 75GB -> 500GB which is fine when you deal with 100MB), etc.
parallelizing my LSH index across multiple processes in Python copies my index (as opposed to using shared mem) so my initial 70 GB index turns into 1 TB+, etc.
for data pipelines: never enough CPU cores, never enough RAM
for training: never enough GPUs, never enough BW
────────

summary:
neat idea! lookahead decoding - they report 1.5-2x speedups during LLM decoding while still being an exact method! amazing way to reduce latency of your LLMs :)
the trick? you have to tradeoff compute for latency: you pay for more FLOPs (exponentially more) but in return you get higher throughput (linearly higher)
given how massively parallel GPUs are more compute doesn't translate into a big overhead in terms of wallclock time and thus the method speeds up decoding
so many old ideas from computer science being built into LLMs (this algo is similar to what CPUs have been doing now for decades to figure out which piece of your code should be executed next)

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Ok - here is a full technical breakdown of what we know about Gemini:
* There are 3 model sizes: Ultra, Pro, Nano. The only disclosed size is for Nano and it's 1.8 & 3.25B. The info is not particularly useful because we could have bound the size given it runs on Pixel.
* Ultra follows Chinchilla scaling laws - as the idea is to get the best possible perf for a given compute budget. Inference was not a concern, PR was, you want bold numbers. Smaller models are all heavily in the data saturation regime.
* Gemini is natively multimodal - i.e. trained from scratch on different modalities.
Compare that with Flamingo whose recipe was:
1) train an LLM - Chinchilla
2) train a vision encoder using contrastive pre-training
3) freeze the backbones and train the system e2e
modality support:
input: text, audio, image, video
output: text, image (a big advantage compared to GPT-4 V)
Multimodal demos:
*
*
* Needless to say the model is massively multilingual as well.
---COMPUTE---
I'll just leave you with this excerpt from the paper:
"but at Gemini Ultra scale, we combine SuperPods in multiple datacenters using Google’s intra-cluster and inter-cluster network.
Google’s network latencies and bandwidths are sufficient to support the commonly used synchronous training paradigm, exploiting model parallelism within superpods and data-parallelism across superpods."
parallelism across GPUs - sweet - how about parallelism across data centers :)
(see below for TPU update)
---EVALS---
* Gemini Ultra’s performance exceeds current SOTA results on 30 of the 32 academic benchmarks BUT IMPORTANT NOTE: not clear how this translates into actual perf given data contamination & in general eval issues with LLMs.
* They report 90% on MMLU which is better than human experts and better than GPT-4 but again it seems the eval methodology was not the same (number of shots + CoT look to be different).
* They report better results than GPT-4V on the new MMMU (multimodal) benchmark.
In general I wouldn't give eval numbers too much attention bc it's not clear whether the comparison is fair between GPT-4 & Gemini - i just want to play with the model. :)
(It's also better than Whisper which is impressive, but:
1) We won't have the weights
2) We have no access to the model
3) We have no idea how much bigger these models are than Whisper in case we ever got the weigths (ok distillation could fix this))
---MISC UPDATES---
* They also share AlphaCode 2 that is estimated to perform better than 85% of codeforces competitive programming competition participants (compared to 50% from original AlphaCode). It leveraged Gemini Pro to get to these results.
* They introduce TPU v5p with 2x more FLOPS and 3x more HBM. A single pod composes of 8960 chips!
* Gemini is already powering many google products (a fine-tuned version of Pro is already in Bard, Nano is running on Pixel)
* On december 13th Pro will be accessible through an API!
Each one of these could be an update in its own right - I simply dislike Google's shipping strategy. It's a firehose method, and if we're talking about safe deployment it's much better to gradually give people access to these systems - a la OpenAI. Just my 2 cents.
And finally: I'm really happy for my ex-colleagues for finally being allowed to show the world what they've been working on. So many familiar names in that long long long contributors section. :)

summary:
Super happy to announce the first ever Serbian LLM eval 🇷🇸 is finally ready! (after the GPT-4 refinement step + manual work) We can now keep track of HBS LLMs progress! Other HBS languages are in the pipeline - but even this one is usable given the similarity of languages.
It's hard to overstate how important this is for the local LLM ecosystem.
Evals are hard, and even more so for low resource languages like Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian, Montenegrin.
You can run the evals using this repo:
The data itself is pulled from HuggingFace here:
I wrote a detailed technical @weights_biases report here if you're curious to learn more about the project and how it was developed:
-- technical TL;DR of the eval --
What is covered?
Common sense reasoning: Hellaswag, Winogrande, PIQA, OpenbookQA, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge
World knowledge: NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA
Reading comprehension: BoolQ
How was the eval created?
3 steps:
1) Machine Translation from English -> Serbian using Google Translate (currently the best system for this lang direction)
2) Refinement via GPT-4 ($$$)
3) Minor manual work by me + we'll likely have a new version of Winogrande that was annotated by a human annotator thanks to @nljubesic!
When I say the project is "finally ready" what I really mean to say is that this is a first usable snapshot! I encourage you to contribute other tasks, you can check out the README for instructions.
This project would be financially very expensive for me if it was not for @weights_biases amazing support, as well as many local individuals & companies who are supporting my work on bootstrapping the local LLM ecosystem. Thank you all! Credits are given on GitHub & HuggingFace.

[3/3] Well, it's official. YugoGPT 7B significantly beats Mistral and LLaMA 2 and is now officially the best open-source LLM in the world for Serbian & other HBS (Croatian, Bosnian, Montenegrin) languages.
Earlier this summer I was frustrated when I saw how poor the situation is as soon as you leave the English NLP space (w/ few exceptions).
Exactly 57 days ago I came up with this idea while working on the Open-NLLB project and training a machine translation system for HBS.
Why not train an LLM for HBS languages? And so yugoGPT was born.
The problem? I had 1 RTX 3090 GPU on my custom built rig. :) (kindly provided to me by @nvidia back in London!)
Fast forward to today I have 16 80 GB A100s from @togethercompute (whom I seriously recommend - not just for their hardware but also for their support & speed & dedication) and 16 more coming in a week (from a different company -> will share more details then).
I had to learn a ton of new stuff as I was basically a single guy (w/ @nljubesic's tremendous help that saved me a ton of time on the data side) building this whole complex system (shout-out to my Discord community was essential for the Serbian LLM eval project).
And I must say: I learned more over the past 6 months than I did during my whole time back at DeepMind. Unless you're very very senior - you just don't get the level of agency I'm enjoying right now.
If I could do this bootstrapped with 16 A100s, give me a cluster of 1000 GPUs and I'll show you how things are getting done :) (hah!) well more on that later, things are cooking in the background.
I'll just say that I'm already working on the 2nd iteration that'll be significantly better.
As for yugoGPT I’ll be red teaming it and I'll need help from the community over the next period to test it. more updates soon :) keep an eye out

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Ok this one is scary 😅 -> Anthropic's new paper shows that once LLMs are trained to be deceptive/malicious the behavior persists even after safety training. And the larger the LLM the better it is at hiding its deceptive behavior.
As a PoC they train a model to write secure code when the prompt states that the year is 2023, but as soon as the year changes to 2024 the model starts outputting exploitable code.
This backdoor persists even after applying SFT (supervised fine-tuning), RLHF (alignment) & adversarial training (eliciting unsafe behavior explicitly & then training to remove it).
It's obvious (at least to me) that we'll ultimately get to a stage where we simply have to trust these models (but we can still build various systems around future super intelligences to somewhat control it). This is the same situation we have today as humans living in the real-world interacting with other humans.
Maybe you interacted with someone whose empathy levels are ~0 (psychopath) and you just didn't know. It's not like we have a choice, we use various heuristics to detect if someone is acting deceptively (body language, etc.), but ultimately all heuristics fail (good book on this topic: What Every BODY is Saying by ex-FBI agent Joe Navarro, tl;dr there is 0 gestures that are 100% indicative of deceptive behavior there are just gestures that indicate the the person is feeling uncomfortable).
The triggers used in the PoC are incredibly simple (2023 -> 2024 is a trigger) but you can imagine this being much more contextual and infinitely more complex.
We'll face very difficult conversations as a society over the upcoming years.
In parallel we'll also get to a point where an image or a video can not be trusted at all (without some special digital signature, etc.). Theoretically there is nothing that's stopping technology from getting to that point (e.g. even the original 2014 GAN paper clearly showed this, distributions of fake & real images ultimately can completely align).
Despite all of this - I don't see an alternative path for technology other then progressing forward (and doing so really fast). The upside is just to big.
Quoting @AnthropicAI
New Anthropic Paper: Sleeper Agents.
We trained LLMs to act secretly malicious. We found that, despite our best efforts at alignment training, deception still slipped through.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GDp2wk1bMAAE_nV.jpg

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Very promising new approach from Meta: Self-Rewarding Language Models that can lead to superhuman agents. The idea is the following:
* Take a "seed" model (in their case LLaMA 2 70B) and teach it to follow instructions using the SFT + EFT datasets based on OpenAssistant. SFT teaches to model how to follow instructions, EFT teaches the model how to reward the prompt-response pairs.
* This model (the "M1" model) is now used in a loop to generate even better iterations (see the attached image below). The loop consists of the following steps:
1) Sample a set of instructions using a fixed model (LLaMA 2-Chat 70B with 8-shot prompting). For all the other steps they use the model that's actually being trained. I suspect that using it here was causing instabilities / mode collapse
2) Generate 4 responses for each instruction using M1 model
3) Evaluate those prompt-response pairs also using M1 model (i.e. assign a 0-5 score to each prompt-response)
4) Form preference pairs and use DPO to get M2
5) Rinse and repeat -> they do this exactly 3 times and each model gets progressively better than the last one
They likely stopped as they observed diminishing returns, but I didn't see any information on this? Likely saving some material for the next paper on the scaling laws.
As always there are issues when evaluating these models. They used AlpacaEval benchmark (that uses GPT-4 in the LLM-as-a-Judge setup against GPT-4-Turbo) that already showed some weird results (like the recent Chinese Yi model outperforming GPT-4).
They don't report any other benchmarks (e.g. lm-evaluation-harness that I used for YugoGPT).
The idea has a strong resemblance to the DeepMind's AlphaGo story: back then the first AlphaGo agent was trained purely on human game data. Later they introduced self-play to go superhuman. It's just a matter of time when we get to that same point with LLMs.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
AlphaCodium - super interesting work that shows just how much alpha (no pun intended) is there from building complex prompt flows in this case for code generation.
It achieves better results than DeepMind's AlphaCode with 4 orders of magnitude fewer LLM calls! This is a direct consequence of the brute force approach that AlphaCode took generating ~100k solutions and then filtering them down (the recently announced AlphaCode2 is much more sample efficient though).
The framework is agnostic to the choice of the underlying LLM. On the validation set with GPT-4 they increase the pass@5 accuracy from 19 -> 44%.
There are 2 steps in the pipeline (and definitely reminds me of Meta's Self-Rewarding Language Models work I shared yesterday):
1) Pre-processing -> transforming the original problem statement into something more concise and parsable by the model, forcing the model to explain the results (why test input leads to a certain output), rank various solutions, etc.
2) Iterative loop where the model fixes its solution code against a set of tests
I feel ultimately we'll want this to be a part of the LLM training process as well and not something we append ad-hoc, but definitely exciting to see how much low hanging fruit is still out there!

[Crypto + AI = solve LLM eval? 🧠] This might be the most creative & interesting effort I've seen recently! An, tbh, likely the only crypto use-case that spiked my interest.
They use crypto to "solve" LLM evaluation issues (as we know how often people game public benchmarks, I've been ranting about this in a lot of my previous posts :)).
Here is how:
1) OSS contributors fine-tune OSS models and publish them to the Bittensor subnet (a decentralized network for AI)
2) A second network (Cortex subnet) continuously generates fresh synthetic tokens produced by GPT-4 and evaluates the models
3) Best models (i.e. their authors) are awarded TAO tokens (the crypto bit)
Need to dig deeper into the project to exactly understand the economics of this. Who is paying for GPT-4, I assume Nous-Bittensor folks might be sponsoring this until it kicks off? If you know more leave a comment below!
Would be good to account for variations in GPT-4 tokens + make sure that version tracking is in place.
Too often people equate open-source with "free". And even more so in less developed markets.
Open-source contributors should be awarded for their work!
Some companies reward their contributors from their revenue pool (I overheard Stability AI might be doing this?) - but most of them give them a tap on the back and say "great work! this community rocks!!" while getting all the financial gains themselves (which always felt unjust).
Will try to closely follow developments of this project.
Quoting @NousResearch
Today we are announcing our latest project, an effort to provide a new evaluation system for open source models. Traditional benchmarking leans heavily on public datasets which can be easy to game and often lead to superficial score improvements that mask true model capabilities (or lack thereof), misdirecting efforts towards meaningless score chasing.
To achieve this, we built a subnet on Bittensor, a decentralized network for AI projects. This system allows you to submit your finetuned model, and then validators will evaluate all models submitted against freshly generated data from the Cortex subnet. The Cortex subnet is a dynamic source of fresh synthetic data, continuously generated by GPT-4, which allows for fresh and unpredictable high quality data to test models against, and ensures a fair and accurate consensus on which model most closely mirrors GPT-4's performance.
This new system aims to celebrate and reward creators of public, open source models that genuinely meet user needs, through the incentive structures built into Bittensor.
We plan to continually evolve and expand the diversity and quality of that continuous data stream over time, to keep the evaluations fresh, challenging, and more and more representative of user needs in every new iteration.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Transformers have become the go-to architecture for LLMs. And more broadly - the whole ML field has converged on transformers (including e.g. computer vision vision after @giffmana's ViT paper was published
But in reality what a lot of folks don't understand is that there is no theory suggesting transformers are the optimal architecture - arguably we've just hit a local optimum in our evolutionary search for better and better architectures (indeed NAS is able to recover more performant architectures but so far at the cost of design complexity).
The reason we use transformers is simply because they have nice compute properties (can be computed in parallel during training compared to e.g. RNNs, etc) and they work well in practice.
Since it's all about having nice properties there have been 2 main new directions I've observed recently:
1) RWKV (shout out to @RWKV_AI)
2) Selective "State Space Models" (SSM)
RWKV is an "attention-less transformer" or an RNN with some nice compute properties e.g. the fact that we don't have to compute it sequentially - which is the property that has been plaguing RNNs since eternity (read since first Schmiedhuber's paper :)) and something that transformers get "for free".
And moreover it has much better inference properties (orders of magnitude faster).
Eagle-7B was just published based on RWKV-v5 architecture, and trained on 1 trillion tokens. It showed similar scaling trends to transformers. It's additionally open-source (Apache license) and it's multilingual (something near and dear to my heart and something we obsess over at Runa AI).
Check out their blog post:
and wiki:
Secondly SSMs have been getting a lot of attention (no pun intended) since @_albertgu & @tri_dao's recent Mamba paper:
With a couple of neat modifications (allowing the model to selectively propagate or forget information along the sequence length dimension depending on the current token and hardware-aware implementation) they retrieved transformer perf with 5x the throughput!
Definitely keep a close eye out on these new architectures.
We still don't know how SSMs behave under the usual "transformer workflows" like fine-tuning, etc. We also don't know how they behave "in the limit" when you scale them upward of 13B - but despite that really promising early results.
Ultimately, as per Rich Sutton's bitter lessons - algorithms that are the most efficient in terms of compute win over the long run. That's why e.g. Flash Attention was such an instant success and had a blazingly fast adoption across the industry.

[🐘🧠 new paper] Suppressing Pink Elephants with Direct Principle Feedback. Do you know about this hack? (see image below) It actually works with humans too. Someone tells you "think whatever you want just don't think about elephants". What's your next thought gonna be? :)
Well - turns out in ML we do have solutions for this class of "failure modes".
A new paper came out handling precisely this:
Why is this important practically speaking? Well put simply - It's a crucial part of instruction-following.
There is a good example from the paper authors:
"If one deploys a chatbot that provides students info about British unis, e.g. you own a company that aids in applying to British unis, it's perhaps not the best decision to help students apply to American unis."
so if you instruct the model never talk about USA universities it should be able to follow that instruction (see the image in the comment below).
Back to the paper - they propose a new method called "Direct Principle Feedback" or DPF for short. It's basically a simplified DPO pipeline (yey!) and for pairs you feed the initial (bad) "response" and a new "revision" (that you get as the output from the critique of the original response).
They show that by applying DPF to OpenHermes-13B (one of powerful Mistral 7B fine-tunes), the model avoids the "Pink Elephant" problem almost as much as GPT-4 does!

summary:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GGQmAbmWQAAdpOR.jpg
Quoting @_jasonwei
An incredible skill that I have witnessed, especially at OpenAI, is the ability to make “yolo runs” work.
The traditional advice in academic research is, “change one thing at a time.” This approach forces you to understand the effect of each component in your model, and therefore is a reliable way to make something work. I personally do this quite religiously. However, the downside is that it takes a long time, especially if you want to understand the interactive effects among components.
A “yolo run” directly implements an ambitious new model without extensively de-risking individual components. The researcher doing the yolo run relies primarily on intuition to set hyperparameter values, decide what parts of the model matter, and anticipate potential problems. These choices are non-obvious to everyone else on the team.
Yolo runs are hard to get right because many things have to go correctly for it to work, and even a single bad hyperparameter can cause your run to fail. It is probabilistically unlikely to guess most or all of them correctly.
Yet multiple times I have seen someone make a yolo run work on the first or second try, resulting in a SOTA model. Such yolo runs are very impactful, as they can leapfrog the team forward when everyone else is stuck.
I do not know how these researchers do it; my best guess is intuition built up from decades of running experiments, a deep understanding of what matters to make a language model successful, and maybe a little bit of divine benevolence. But what I do know is that the people who can do this are surely 10-100x AI researchers. They should be given as many GPUs as they want and be protected like unicorns.

summary:
Had a lot of people ask for it so here it is: a comparison between YugoGPT (7B) vs Aya-101 (13B) - a recent multilingual LLM from Cohere!
First of all a massive congrats & thank you to the Cohere team for organizing the Aya data effort! Their data effort is something the whole world should be grateful for!
Now onto the comparison -> since I last published YugoGPT base model results (which significantly outperformed Mistral & LLaMA) I've been cooking new LLMs internally together with Fei Yu (our PhD intern working on alignment) on our freshly acquired 16 H100s from @Hyperstackcloud!❤️
[ A big thank you to the team for the amazing support! We are also seeing 2x perf for our LLM workloads compared to A100s - I strongly suggest you give them a try! :) ]
The new instruct & align models are much more powerful - which reflects in quantitative metrics on Serbian LLM eval (see the chart below):
1) You can see that across the board our new internal models outperform YugoGPT base
2) You can see that even YugoGPT base significantly outperforms Aya-101 on all the tasks!
[ Note that Aya has an outlier performance on the boolq task and our align models are a bit weaker (compared to our instruct models) on triviaqa & nq_open - we are looking into this ]
More importantly the difference is even bigger on qualitative metrics. For one - yugochat ( is powered by our internal instruct models - and we already got amazing feedback from native speakers using it "in the wild" :)
Secondly - I did play with Aya-101 and quickly concluded that it doesn't really work well for Serbian. :/
That's not surprising though.
It's obvious that you can't train a massively multilingual (101 languages) dense transformer (fine-tune of mT5) the way they did and expect to have interesting performance on any particular language (esp. not with 13B params).
MoE approach would certainly work better esp. with some special language conditioning tokens - but with a big tradeoff one has to make in both cases -> a much lower efficiency (in terms of model size / vocab table bloat).
The way I see the future of multilingual models is we need multilingual models but scoped down to support narrow language families. That's what I'm building at Runa AI and that's what YugoGPT is for BCS languages (and more langs coming very soon).
That's a wrap!
--- appendix
I believe that Cohere team built Aya-101 13B model more as an academic exercise to showcase how their data (which is the main thing here really) improves mT5 (which is the base model they use as the starting point) and achieves new SOTA on average across those 101 languages.
The model is Apache 2.0 which is super cool!
One confusing bit for me is: the translations have been created using the NLLB model which is for non-commercial use only - so I'm not sure whether its output is under a permissive license?
They had 3 variants of their model depending on how they weight their data sources and decided to go with "translated-heavy" Aya at the end (which over-indexes on translation datasets).

summary:
DeepMind just announced Gemini 1.5 Pro. You can't try it yet (:sadface:) but here is a brief technical summary as the results hint at an incredible future (:happyface:)
First of all it's a MoE model (similar to Mixtral), and it's likely a distill of their Ultra 1.0 model (as it required only a fraction of the training cost)
It has a "1M" token multimodal context length (there is no upper bound really 1M is semi-arbitrarily picked as the "official context lenght" based on recall threshold).
You can put in entire books, whole codebases, movies, etc.
They say this is the first LLM that supports this many tokens but we already had OSS models achieve this, it's just that among proprietary LLM providers the max so far was 200k (Claude from @AnthropicAI).
They do needle in a haystack synthetic tests where you place a bit of information somewhere in the context and expect the model to retrieve that info through a query. The results look impressive, but not sure how well this translates into actual performance that people care about. The impressive bit is that since the model is multimodal they can do this for audio, video, text!
The speeds right now are not really usable for now (~ 1 minute) - but I'm really happy they've been honest in their marketing this time!
One impressive demonstration of what's to come: they take a 45 min video and embed a single frame per second into the model (~684k tokens) and then ask "Tell me some key information from the piece of paper that is removed from the person’s pocket, and the timecode of that moment." and the model replies correctly.
Again take everything with a grain of salt it might be cherry picked and it likely is, but still -> hints at a bright future that's coming :))
They also show multimodal queries where they input an abstract drawing and ask a question "Look at the event in this drawing. What page is this on?"
This has a massive potential to improve the way we do search!
One more example I really loved is the Kalamang translation. :)) It's a lang spoken by fewer than 200 speakers?? and it has almost no online presence.
There is only one book called "A Grammar of Kalamang" that they input into the model together with a bilingual wordlist and the model learns to translate from English to/from Kalamang. Super cool.

Extremely cool new model release from @AI21Labs - Jamba - and it's not even a transformer! It's a hybrid model that combines Mamba (structured state space model), transformer layers and MoE technique, and it's a first production-grade Mamba based model!
* It's a 52B MoE with 12B params active during inference.
* Due to it being Mamba-based it has a much better throughput and efficiency.
* 3x throughput on long contexts compared to Mixtral.
* It has a 256k context window! Out of those 140k context can be achieved on a single GPU which makes it much easier to deploy.
* Perf-wise it looks to be on-par with Mixtral.
* It's open-weight model (licensed under Apache 2.0)
Really exciting, this is apparently the first time someone scaled Mamba upward from 3B. 52B it is. :)

If you're still struggling to understand how transformers work here are some amazing resources! (including mine! :))
First of all @3blue1brown just released 2 videos covering in fair amount of depth word embeddings, transformers and its submodules like embedding mechanism, attention mechanism, MLP, softmax, etc:
Also, I'd supplement that with my original transformer implementation in PyTorch here:
With close to 1000 stars it looks like that project was very impactful! :) I invested the extra effort to nicely comment every single operation in the multi-head attention module and beyond.
Back to 3B1B - I just watched the videos yesterday and still managed to get something out of it.
Namely I never thought of the output attention matrix as a bottleneck transformation.
The way it's implemented misguided my conceptual understanding of what's happening there.
You can think of the value vectors at a particular position from all the MHA heads just being concatenated and mapped using the DxD matrix (where D is internal model dim) before passing the representations to MLP - which is not really insightful - or you can think of it first being mapped into the model dimension space and later summed up across all MHA heads.
It's subtle but makes a big difference in understanding of what's going on if you grok the underlying linear algebra.
Grant is an artist. You can not not love his work. Happy learning!

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Very cool recent paper "Better & Faster LLMs via Multi-token Prediction". The main idea is to modify LLM's objective function such that we predict not 1 but N next tokens conditioned on the past tokens.
The extension is conceptually fairly simple and I've read some transformer papers already back in ~2019/2020 that have done these ablations on a *smaller* scale - BUT - we know that conclusions won't necessarily extrapolate to the *large* model regime.
But in practice this extension is extremely cool for multiple reasons:
1) Turns out they can improve the perf of the model (they demonstrate significant improvement on code benchmarks (MBPP) and the bigger the model the higher the gain - surprise, surprise!).
I'm not completely sure whether they've normalized the results with FLOPs/number of params in these calculations though, otherwise the gains might be overestimated.
2) You get speculative decoding "for free"! Instead of having a smaller LM offer a hypothesis that's then verified by the large LM here in a single pass you already get those next n tokens! This yields a nice speedup during inference!
They've done certain memory optimizations (given that now you'd be potentially generating 'N*vocab_size' numbers in the output due to logits being of 'vocab_size' length) that made sure there is no significant hit in terms of memory/runtime with this method.
Paper:

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Interesting paper from DeepMind: "Many-Shot In-Context Learning".
The research consists of analyzing how long-context models (they only used Gemini 1.5 Pro with 1M context window) behave when we go from the "few-shot" regime to the "many-shot" regime where they stuff in hundreds or thousands of examples (as opposed to tens of examples with "few-shot").
Given that it's hard to always fit in purely human-generated "shots" they explore 2 ways to scale the context:
1) Reinforced method - uses model-generated CoT (chain-of-thought) rationales instead of human generated ones.
2) Unsupervised method - removes the rationales altogether and prompts the model only with domain-specific inputs/problems and a few problem-solution pairs at the end (see appendix A6 of the paper for the exact format).
Not surprisingly the model improves across a variety of tasks including translation, summarization, problem solving, etc.
There are some caveats though:
* Sometimes the peformance does degrade with more examples - they didn't provide an explanation; but could be as simple as garbage in/garbage out?
Many-shot helps the model "locate its internal knowledge" but if you misguide it it gives you worse garbage. It'll be interesting research area how to design the many-shot context properly.
* Similarly to few-shot - many-shot is still very sensitive to the ordering of the input examples.
Paper:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GNnva2YWQAAwBzv.jpg

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
[tech summary] Meta just announced a new multimodal transformer - 🦎 Chameleon! Interestingly enough they report 60.4% preference rate against Gemini-Pro+ and 51.6% against GPT-4V+!
Big caveat here: + means these baselines are hybrid ones. They took e.g. Gemini that only receives multimodal input and prompted it to generate <caption>...</caption> when the question asks it to generate an image (as it can't generate an image directly though the API).
Subsequently that caption is fed into DALL-E 3 and finally that image is used to replace the original <caption>...</caption>. That's the actual baseline they compared against. Still impressive results.
Re architecture - it closely follows Llama 2 / Mistral (the usual stuff: RMSNorms instead of LayerNorms, RoPE positional encoding, SwiGLU activation function in the MLP layer...).
Chameleon was trained on 10T multimodal tokens (text only, text-image, multiple images interspersed with text).
They trained an image tokenizer (fun fact they upsampled human faces 2 times, but apparently not as good with generating text) and they trained new BPE text tokenizer with ~65.5k tokens. As a consequence they use a single transformer to train their model, and they feed it text/img tokens.
They had issues with instabilities during training with multimodal data with models in the 8B+ params and 1T+ tokens regime, happening very late in training.
They observed that growth of norms strongly correlated with divergence.
Strategies they deployed:
* QK norm (layer norm applied to Q and K within attn mechanism before computing the scores)
* dropout (esp. after the attn softmax)
* z-loss regularization (regularizing the partition function Z, i.e. denominator of softmax) for the final softmax layer
* reordering of RMS norms was important (post-normalization as opposed to pre-norm)
All in all, a strong signal that Meta is catching up with its multimodal research!
Paper:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GN3FzozXUAAwK9o.jpg

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Optimizing LLM inference is extremely important nowadays. Here are the core ideas behind Orca and PagedAttention (vLLM) papers. But first - why do we care?
Well, by optimizing your serving engine you're:
1) Increasing throughput - which means more users can use your service per unit of time
2) Decreasing latency - which means your app is snapier for individual users
3) Reducing the AI accelerator cost - i.e. more $$$ in your bank account :)
Let's dig into the core ideas.
***Orca***
The core idea behind Orca is continuous batching.
To appreciate it let's first understand what naive batching looks like:
* When a new request arrives it has to wait for the previous batch of requests to finish their decoding. This waiting unnecessarily increases its latency.
* When one of the requests in the batch has emitted an EOS token it still has to wait for the slowest request in the batch to finish - which again, increases its latency.
What Orca does is after every single fwd pass it checks whether any of the requests is done processing or if we have any new requests waiting - and thus it dynamically updates what requests are going to be processed next.
The problem here is that we have requests that are in different phases of execution (prefill or incremental decoding) and of different sequence lengths (prefill) or at a different position in the sequence (inc. decoding).
To work around this problem Orca additionally introduces "selective batching".
The cool thing about transformers is that other than the core attn layer all other ops can be executed pointwise (MLP, hidden-to-logit Linear, LayerNorm, etc.).
Exploiting this property they flatten the batch dimension, i.e. concat across the sequence dimension and only then do a fwd pass (i.e. requests with shapes (seq len,hidden dim)=(3, 256) and (7, 256) become (10,256).
Immediately before the attn layer they split this tensor to run attn on a per request basis (with those sequences in the inc. decoding stage additionally attending their KV cache), and after it they immediately merge and continue with the previous flattened tensor logic.
This splitting has to be done because tokens from a single sequence should not attend tokens from a different sequence.
***PagedAttention***
KV cache is one of the main bottlenecks when running inference as you have to load it together with model weights in each step during your incremental decoding (causing memory-bw-bottleneck).
Naive implementations simply statically allocate max-seq-len KV vectors for each request (that can be e.g. 2048). Most of those remain unoccupied as most requests might end after e.g. 20 tokens.
What PagedAttention paper did was they borrowed the concept of paging & virtual memory from OS literature and chunked KV cache into blocks. Doing this the memory waste is upper bounded by the block size (usually 16-32 tokens). This is a huge saving! You resolve inner and external fragmentation issues.
Obviously to support PagedAttention they know had to introduce the concepts of logical and physical memory blocks and they had to implement custom CUDA kernels to make attention computation efficient (due to blocks being non-contiguous in the memory).
The latency increase of their attn logic is only ~20% but the end to end perf of the system is drastically improved as they now support much bigger batch sizes that leads to higher throughput.
These ideas deserve a blog post, which i might write over the next few weeks.
There is a ton more you can do here to optimize inference:
* GQA - to reduce the size of your KV cache (that's why Mistral & Llama use it)
* quantization to int8/int4 (and lower?) to reduce the memory bandwidth pressure
* speculative decoding - compute k next tokens using a draft model and then run the full model only once to verify correct tokens
etc. etc.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
[tech summary of RingAttention] Ever wondered how Google Gemini provides you with 1-2M context windows?
Although I can only speculate (I assume that most of the current DeepMinders don't know it as well as these details are kept secret nowadays) here is a way of how it *could* be done:
Combine:
1) RingAttention (that's based off of FlashAttention + previous BPT work (see below))
2) N TPUs/GPUs (where N acts as a context length multiplier)
3) smart positional embedding methods (RoPE-derivatives, e.g. see YaRN paper)
RingAttention is based on 2 previous works:
1) FlashAttention (FA) - that basically avoids materializing N^2 probability matrix inside of the self-attn layer (and thus achieving O(N) memory) by combining tiling with online softmax. All that is implemented in CUDA and requires understanding the details of NVIDIA's hardware (main bit being: HBM (DRAM) access is expensive, deal with shared memory (SRAM) as much as possible).
(see my technical blog explanation here:
2) Blockwise Parallel transformer (BPT) that builds upon FA idea and applies the same tiling reasoning to the FFN layer (that goes immediately after self-attn layer in the transformer layer). This allowed them to reduce the activation cost from 8bsh to 2bsh (~4x mem saving! which translates to ~4x context length increase!).
Now for the fun part - RingAttention (RA)!
On a high level RA allows you to scale up your context length by N, where N is the number of TPUs/GPUs you've got available.
Cool, but how?
It connects all devices into a ring topology with N devices, takes the input sequence and splits it into N chunks and assignes each chunk to a single device.
That device is subsequently responsible for computing queries, keys, and values for only that chunk.
Now for the fun part.
The i-th device computes local scores using its local QKV and concurrently sends its KV chunk to the (i+1)-th device while receiving a new KV chunk from (i-1)-th device. Rinse and repeat N-1 times in a circular / ring fashion and thanks to the permutation invariance of attn coupled with computing the statistics properly (see FA work) each device ends up with a correct result!
Now, as per bitter lessons, all of this would be for nothing if we can't do it efficiently. The important point is to overlap computation & communication so that we end up with 0 overhead.
Turns out that per-device computation requires f=4*d*c^2 FLOPs
and at each step of the ring-logic we have to send b=2*c*d bytes (c - block size, d - dimensionality, 2 - bf16/fp16).
In order to mask the communication overhead we need:
f/F (time to compute) > b/B (time to send data)
where F - peak FLOPs (e.g. 312 TFlops for A100 when dealing with bf16) and B - max memory bandwidth.
That gives us that c (block size) must be >= F/B.
Under that assumption there is 0 overhead and you can potentially scale to 10M+ context lengths. :) Voila!
In practice this means that for e.g. A100 with an NVLink the minimum block size is ~1000 and min sequence length is 6x that.
In general the only part I didn't fully grok is how they got the s=6*c rule (i.e. seq len must be at least 6x the block size). If anyone figured it out lmk in the comment below!
Ring-attn paper:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GORlyQQXkAAUDq1.jpg

fun experiment - water-fasting for 3 full days (72 hours)
my only intake were water, cup of tea before sleep, and a glass of lemonade when i wake up
daily workout routine:

5x15 straight leg sit-ups
couple of sets of pull-ups/push-ups (had some strain that's indicative of upcoming injury so had to modify my routine)
stretching
2 km run back home
cold shower after the workout
other than that just working morning to midnight quite intensively
learnings?
* first of all we can definitely push ourselves much much more than we think
* it's completely wild that until this year (i'm 29) i've never had a single day in my life where I didn't put anything in my stomach - so many experiments ahead of me :) the breadth & depth of human experience is immense
* day 3 is when i started feeling tired walking upstairs, which was a good sign i should start wrapping this experiment up - even though i felt i could definitely push for many more days
* in chill mode (no intensive workouts, no work) i could easily go 7+ days
* we eat mostly out of habit, e.g. when we're bored, or when the clock says so - we don't listen to our bodies at all
* my focus was incredibly good, and i didn't feel my blood sugar was too low (other than morning of day 3 when i felt it, but after the workout felt much better, could be just because i had a prolonged sitting session?)
* can't imagine how it looks like to be chronically starved, i did feel a bit of a stomach pain from hunger in a couple of occasions - also - it's much different when i do it voluntary vs when you're forced not to eat obviously
* we should teach our kids to fast every once in a while, and not for religious reasons, just for strengthening the character / self-control and apparently for some health benefits :)

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
[LLM.int8() tech summary] Ever wondered how LLM int8 inference in HuggingFace/bitsandbytes works or just in general? How can you run a 175B param models with no degradation while using only [-128, 127] (int8) range?
First of all for some background context that helps appreciate the fact that this even works:
LLMs nowadays are mostly trained in fp16/bf16/fp32 mixed precision. That means they're "used to seeing" numbers up to e.g. 3.39*10^38 (in bf16), but during inference you force the activations & weights into the [-128, 127] range, and things...just work? :)
The answer is: well yes, but it's not trivial to pull it off, esp. for LLMs that have a lot of params.
The main reason why previous quantization methods didn't work in the large scale regime is that fact that around ~7B param threshold (6.7B in the paper) a phase shift happens.
What happens is an emergence of outlier features that are e.g. 20x+ larger than other features in other dimensions. And they're extremely sparse (e.g. 7 out of 4096 features are affected).
If you try something like absmax quantization those features will make all the other features collapse basically to zero. That happens because we divide the vector by the absmax value and then multiply by 127 & round to nearest int in order to bring them into int8 range. If most numbers were around e.g. 0.5-3.5 and your outlier is 70.3 you crush those other features after the quantization.
So what's the solution?
There are 2 parts to it. First of all we mostly care about matmul operation as that's where most of the flops & params are.
How matrix multiplication computation is done on the actual GPU is in a embarrassingly parallel fashion where you do dot products between rows and columns at the same time.
(obv. this is a simplification, there is tiling and there is caching to GPU's shared memory (SRAM) but this level of understanding is good enough for the sake of my explanation).
Back to what the 2 parts are:
1) We first do the so-called vector-wise quantization. Where you absmax normalize all rows & columns of your 2 matrices independently (as opposed to having e.g. a single scalar for the whole matrix). You then convert them into the int8 range, you do the dot product and accumulate into int32 (so you don't overflow).
To dequantize you just undo the normalization (elementwise product with the outer product of column and row scaling coefficients you previously computed).
The problem is this approach works only until we hit ~2.7B param scale!
2) The second crucial part is "mixed-precision decomposition", i.e. do the same computation except that this time you split your rows & columns such that the ones that have outliers (big numbers) are extracted and they undergo 16 bit dot-product - otherwise 8 bit.
Most dot products will be 8-bit (as outliers are extremely sparse) so we still get ~2x memory saving!
That's it in a nutshell. Obviously to make this efficient you have to write your custom CUDA kernels! :) GPU go brrrr.
This is one of my favorite papers btw:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GOWx-kSW4AA8xBH.jpg

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
I just posted about LLM.int8() but turns out there is an even better int8 method that's super recent - SmoothQuant! Here are the main ideas:
LLM.int8() already pointed out that the issue are outlier features across some of the channels (it's very sparse, only a few channels are affected).
Their solution was to compute the dot products for affected vectors in fp16 instead of using int8 and thus avoiding having to quantize them.
The issue is: it's very hard to implement this efficiently, so even though LLM.int8() had ~2x mem reduction its latency results are suboptimal, and only for the biggest of the models it showed a tiny bit of improvement compared to the fp16 baseline, otherwise it's mostly slower!
(curious to hear whether Tim had some perf improvements since?)
SmoothQuant solved this in a mathematically more elegant way and achieves much superior latency! (while keeping 2x mem reduction)
How does it work?
The high level idea is that even though activations (X) suffer from these outliers, actual LLM weights (W) in linear layers do not. So let's try and rebalance them? :)
We're computing the following in a linear layer:
Y = X@W (@ == matmul)
That's mathematically equivalent with:
Y = (X @ diag(S)^(-1)) @ (diag(S) @ W)
(Since matmul is associative you can easily see that inverse diag(S) matrix will give you identity (I) matrix when multiplied with diag(S))
The nice computational property of diagonal (hence "diag") matrices is that they basically act as column-wise scalars.
Example:
X = [[3, 232],
[2, 180]]
S = [[1/3, 0],
[0, 1/232]]
you end up with:
Y = [[1, 1],
[2/3, 180/232]]
So we can use S to scale those outlier channels to a normal range!
This can be very efficiently implemented by doing "kernel fusion" (see my flash attention blog for an explanation so that this is basically as expensive as computing X@W without diag(S). Great!
So now we're left with 2 questions:
1) How do we compute S?
2) How do we quantize our weights & activations after applying 1)?
S is computed by passing a small number of sentences from your dataset through your target LLM (they used only ~512 from the Pile), observing the activations (X) and computing the absmax values across the channel dimension 'd' (X shape = [s,d], W shape = [d, d_out]).
You repeat the same for your W matrix finding absmax across rows.
To compute S you divide those 2 vectors and use a single hyperparam (alpha) to decide how much should absmax values from X vs W have an impact on the final S_j.
This makes sure we don't make W hard to quantize because we "spilled" too much of the "outlier dynamics" to it.
After this you can simply quantize the tensors W & X using either per tensor or per vector absmax that you can precompute on those same 512 sentences and reuse during runtime (turns out this works just well!).
The crazy thing they show is they're serving a 530B model within a single node (8 GPUs) with lower latency and same accuracy compared to fp16 baseline (that needs 16 GPUs and is slower!).
This saves you 2x $. :)

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
A few words on how to optimize GPU applications for both training / serving use-cases and save $$$:
Inefficiencies creep in across one of these 3 dimensions:
1) {Python, PyTorch, kernel launch} overhead
2) FLOPs
3) Memory bandwidth (host<->device, device<->device, HBM<->SRAM)
[Re 3) I'll focus only on HBM<->SRAM here: for the host<->device you have to be smart with your memory pinning and for the device<->device have good HW interconnects and be smart about what data you communicate]
How do we optimize these 3 bottlenecks?
### Overhead
First of all what is it?
It's your python interpreter, it's your PyTorch framework trying to figure out which GPU kernel to launch (depending on the dimensions of your matrix, its dtype, target GPU type (RTX4090, A100, H100...), etc.), and it's the actual overhead associated with the CPU/GPU-side kernel launch.
To reduce the overhead there is a couple of techniques people use:
a) Don't use Python - use C/C++ (obviously you're giving away flexibility and ease of prototyping here)
b) jit tracing or CUDA graphs (lower level, but similar semantics) - which basically, as the word suggests, trace out all the decisions that your framework made in the first iteration (e.g. what GPU kernel to use) without having to rerun that same logic again. Just replay.
### FLOPs
a) Make sure most of your FLOPs come from bf16/fp16 (or lower precision) matmul as that's where the highest FLOPs/sec throughput is, that's what NVIDIA is optimizing.
b) Reduce FLOPs by being smarter with your maths (e.g. see FlashAttention 2 paper for some examples) or shard
c) Buy better HW with higher FLOPs/sec!
### Mem BW (this is where most optimizations truly happen)
I'll focus mostly on inference latency.
Basically during every single decode step you have to:
1) Load your model weights
2) Load KV cache
3) Compute the fwd pass
Let's see how the model bandwidth formula looks like:
(num_params * num_bytes_per_param * tokens/sec) / (mem_bw)
Where num_params is KV cache + model weights.
How do we minimize this?
1) Reduce number of params! :)
1.1) Model distillation
1.2) Weight pruning (rarely used afaik)
2) Reduce number of bytes in your weights:
2.1) Quantize your weights to 8 bits or less
2.2) Don't use the big model use the draft model (speculative decoding)
3) Reduce your KV cache:
3.1) Use MQA/GQA (that's how Mistral/Llama, etc. save up 4x)
3.2) Quantize the cache activations
3.3) Make sure you're not wasting memory by using static KV cache logic (e.g. use PagedAttention)
4) Increase your mem bandwidth N times by using N GPUs (tensor parallelism).
5) Reduce HBM(DRAM)<->SRAM data movement (kernel fusion)
6) Optimize your attn mechanism:
6.1) Use sparse patterns (allows you to skip blocks in your CUDA kernels to reduce computation)
6.2) Flash Attention 2
7) Quantize activations
I think those are the main techniques on top of my head, lmk know in the comments if I missed any significant one!

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Incredibly unexpected and super cool fact about NVIDIA GPUs: matrix multiplication speed depends on the content of your matrices! :) Surprised? Read on!
(note: it's not only for NVIDIA GPUs but i'll use them as the running example)
This is one of those moments when your software stack is a leaky abstraction for the underlying hardware.
Conceptually, if we were in the "Platonic world of ideas", the speed (FLOPs / sec) should only be a function of the shapes of your matrices.
If matrix A is of shape (m,n) and B is of shape (n,k) then the speed with which we compute C = A @ B (@ == matmul) of shape (m,k) should only be a function of m,n, and k, i.e. f(m,n,k).
At least that's what a reasonable ML engineer / scientist expects.
But why is this not actually the case?
The answer lies in the fact that GPUs are power limited, they are designed to operate under certain power thresholds (see e.g. TDP), and power is a function of your GPU clock frequency and the switching frequency of the underlying transistors.
Roughly P = clk_freq * switch_freq.
The more the transistors switch (as you feed them alternating voltage that corresponds to your positive / negative numbers), the more current is flowing through your chip and the so-called dynamic dissipation power increases (as opposed to the static dissipation that happens no matter whether the transistors are switching or not).
So it turns out that if you multiply a matrix with all 0s you end up with less switching, your GPU doesn't get power-throttled and the clock frequency remains stable (and thus your FLOPs / sec).
But if you use a matrix initialized with random numbers (esp. Gaussian) you end up with more switching which causes the GPU to drop the clock frequency in order to stay under the power threshold and this reduces your FLOPs / sec!!
Unless you're deep into optimizing your ML/LLM software stack you mostly won't care about this. Similar to how compiler quirks can sometimes impact your software behavior, but the majority of programmers will never ever have to think about it.
But it's still fun to know, and as a bonus, you'll be fun at parties. :') (maybe in SF?)
Ultimately an amazing metric to track GPU efficiency is how much compute you can squeeze out for a given amount of power: FLOPs / watt.
That's the gist of it.
If you want to know more @cHHillee wrote a more in-depth explanation of the phenomenon here:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GO6eM5JW8AASMBQ.jpg

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
New paper - "Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings" shows that transformers are better on arithmetic tasks than you might think!
Brief context:
Ever since the GPT-3 paper came out back in May 2020 ( and showed that GPT-3 (despite being trained on 10.000 V100s and having 175B params) is still struggling with even 3 digit addition people have been talking how this is some fundamental limitation of these systems and how we need to code in explicit world models or what not (plug in your favorite midwit meme).
Since then we understood that a lot of that actually has to do with tokenizers (e.g. you, the human, see 23200 + 17239 but GPT-3 sees "232", "00", "+", "1", "72", "39" - i.e. chunks that don't even correspond to single digits) and less with the fundamental limitations on the side of LLMs and how we train them.
Making sure that tokenizers tokenize numbers into single digit constituents was important.
This paper additionally shows that being smart with embeddings (they add an embedding to each digits that encodes its position relative to the start of the number, basically encoding the positional number system) boosts the performance quite a bit.
They show that training on only 20 digits numbers with a single GPU for only 1 day reaches SOTA results! 99% accuracy on 100 digit addition!
They further show that this benefits other multi-step reasoning problems (sorting, multiplication...).
What a time to be alive. Progress is happening daily it's just that public perceives it as happening in quants ("AlexNet moment", "ChatGPT moment", etc).
Note: didn't read the paper in great depth, not 100% confident that there are no gotchas here, I'll keep you posted.
