@imbue_ai just published an extremely informative blog post on how they built their 4000+ H100 machine cluster! They also shared some of the health/stress-testing scripts they developed to make sure their servers are operational 24/7.
In total they have 511 nodes (8xH100 each) connected into a fully nonblocking fat tree InfiniBand network topology (see the attached image) consisting of 3 levels:
T1 - this is where the 511 hosts are at
T2 - 128 "leaves" network switches
T3 - 128 "spines" switches
T4 - 64 "super spines"
They had to do everything from scratch including install the OS images on all the machines.
Interestingly enough a staggering 10% of the machines failed to boot due to various hardware errors (unconnected/miswired Ethernet cables, bad NVME drives, etc.).
Next up after installing the sw stack they started running single node trainings and debugging individual nodes making sure they work before going into multi-node training runs. And then growing the "golden set" of servers that are reliably working:
"A rule of thumb for GPU clusters using the newest hardware: expect about 3% of machines to break every week.
There is a crucial nuance that often gets lost, however: it’s not that every machine has a uniform 3% chance of failing; rather, a small number of malcontent machines repeatedly break in different ways until they’re properly fixed. "
They have a lots of great tips on diagnosing common training issues during startup or during the run itself, including runs hanging (had fun with NCCL hangs/timeouts myself over the past period :')). And even more sneaky are training slowdowns (MFU).
Great read even if you don't want to manage your own cluster.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
working with Andrej and a few cracked engineers over the past period has been a blast
llm.c ftw 🫡
Quoting @karpathy
In 2019, OpenAI announced GPT-2 with this post:
Today (~5 years later) you can train your own for ~$672, running on one 8XH100 GPU node for 24 hours. Our latest llm.c post gives the walkthrough in some detail:
Incredibly, the costs have come down dramatically over the last 5 years due to improvements in compute hardware (H100 GPUs), software (CUDA, cuBLAS, cuDNN, FlashAttention) and data quality (e.g. the FineWeb-Edu dataset). For this exercise, the algorithm was kept fixed and follows the GPT-2/3 papers.
Because llm.c is a direct implementation of GPT training in C/CUDA, the requirements are minimal - there is no need for conda environments, Python interpreters, pip installs, etc. You spin up a cloud GPU node (e.g. on Lambda), optionally install NVIDIA cuDNN, NCCL/MPI, download the .bin data shards, compile and run, and you're stepping in minutes. You then wait 24 hours and enjoy samples about English-speaking Unicorns in the Andes.
For me, this is a very nice checkpoint to get to because the entire llm.c project started with me thinking about reproducing GPT-2 for an educational video, getting stuck with some PyTorch things, then rage quitting to just write the whole thing from scratch in C/CUDA. That set me on a longer journey than I anticipated, but it was quite fun, I learned more CUDA, I made friends along the way, and llm.c is really nice now. It's ~5,000 lines of code, it compiles and steps very fast so there is very little waiting around, it has constant memory footprint, it trains in mixed precision, distributed across multi-node with NNCL, it is bitwise deterministic, and hovers around ~50% MFU. So it's quite cute.
llm.c couldn't have gotten here without a great group of devs who assembled from the internet, and helped get things to this point, especially ademeure, ngc92, @gordic_aleksa, and rosslwheeler. And thank you to @LambdaAPI for the GPU cycles support.
There's still a lot of work left to do. I'm still not 100% happy with the current runs - the evals should be better, the training should be more stable especially at larger model sizes for longer runs. There's a lot of interesting new directions too: fp8 (imminent!), inference, finetuning, multimodal (VQVAE etc.), more modern architectures (Llama/Gemma). The goal of llm.c remains to have a simple, minimal, clean training stack for a full-featured LLM agent, in direct C/CUDA, and companion educational materials to bring many people up to speed in this awesome field.
Eye candy: my much longer 400B token GPT-2 run (up from 33B tokens), which went great until 330B (reaching 61% HellaSwag, way above GPT-2 and GPT-3 of this size) and then exploded shortly after this plot, which I am looking into now :)

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] LLaMA 3.1 LLMs are out! :) Multilingual, coding, tool usage! The largest one is 405B params with a context len of 128k! Both base+instruct models are released.
They're claimining on-par perf with GPT-4 according to MMLU, HumanEval, MATH, and other evals. Looking forward to see how these models perform in the wild!
The architecture is basically the same as previous Llamas with minor modifications (RoPE base freq changed to 500k, vocab size 128k (tiktoken + 28k to support multilinguality)).
LLaMA 3 405 was trained on 16k H100s! 15.6 trillion tokens were used for pretraining with 8k context length.
To get from 8k->128k they have 6 stages where they gradually increase the context length and observe whether the model learned to use the additional tokens (via needle in haystack experiments). They used ~800B tokens for this.
During the very end of the pretraining stage they anneal learning rate down to 0 and form the final checkpoint as the average of model checkpoints during the annealing procedure (Polyak averaging).
License: LLaMA 3 community license. You're allowed to use the outputs even from the 405B to improve your models! SX data go brrrr. :))
Supported languages: English, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, Hindi, Spanish, and Thai (+ they did train on more langs, but these have been evaluated).
Internally they computed isoFLOP curves for compute budget in the range: [6x10^18, 6x10^22] FLOPs.
After fitting a curve on the minimum of all parabolas they end up that for their compute budget the optimal params are 405B and ~16.5T tokens.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
🔥 Extremely cool work from the @PyTorch team! FlexAttention API! Listen in, this will likely benefit all PyTorch users!
-> So far if you wanted to experiment with new attention mechanisms, and PyTorch didn't have a ready Triton/CUDA kernel for you, well, you were out of luck:
1) You either have to accept the HW lottery and deal with much lower perf compared to hyperoptimized attn baselines (Flash Attention et al)
2) Or you have to roll up your sleeves and write a CUDA/Triton kernel implementation yourself instead of writting a high level PyTorch imp (or hire someone to do it for you :)).
FlexAttention solves this for PyTorch ecosystem!
They made a simple API whereby you just have to implement a "score_mod" function in Python, telling FlexAttention API how you want to combine your queries and keys (i.e. how to modify your attn scores), and it automatically lowers your high level implementation to a single fused, thus highly efficient kernel!
You want regular attention?
"score_mod" is just an identity function (well in this case you'll won't use FlexAttention but you get the sense of generality & simplicity of the API whereby regular attn is just a special case).
You want relative position encodings, you just implement this:
def relative_positional(score, b, h, q_idx, kv_idx):
return score + (q_idx - kv_idx)
There is one more important concept to learn and it's "mask_mod" but i refer you to the excellent blog post linked below for more info.
TL;DR: it's dead simple to implement various attentions like Alibi, soft-capping (popularized by Gemma/Grok), sliding window (popularized by Mistral 7B), prefix attn, jagged attn, or really any combination (causal + sliding, etc.).
So what's the catch? There must be some tradeoff?
That's right, there is an overhead cost you have to pay. You get a bit lower perf compared to a dedicated hyperoptimized kernel (85-90% there for A100s and they're working on it for H100s) but there is a huge gain in generality and ease of use!
I think it hits a great sweat spot for researchers and allows for exploration of new ideas.
Once you need to go to prod, and small % of effieciency increase translate to $ Ms for your business - well in that case you can pay your GPU programmers to save you those $ Ms. :)
But most smaller companies won't care (and won't be able to afford GPU experts) and this will be a game changer for them.
Having said all of that FlexAttention still has some rough edges:
* Only available in nightly releases
* Sequence lengths must be multiples of 128 (this propagates up to you as a user all the way from the actual hardware)
* GQA support is missing
etc. but should be good for many interesting use-cases already!
Have fun:

While USA/China are treating energy as a currency (which it is) and are competing for a massive build-out to support the increasing needs of AI (among other priorities) - EU, and Germany in particular, are falling for the de-accelerationist propaganda and are destroying all of their nuclear power plants.

Steel, concrete, plastics, ammonia (needed for nitrogenous-fertilizers and thus food production), the pillars of our material civilization, and now increasingly AI, all require an exorbitant amount of energy. You can't be a sovereign nation without a powerful & robust energy system.
What happened to the nuclear technology is a great tragedy of our era, a story of anti-progress and fear-mongering, and a similar faith might happen to AI (with recent California's SB1047 bill, EU AI act, etc.).
Great potential benefits are overlooked and down-weighted as people focus too much on the potential harms of technology.
I don't think it's widely known that new nuclear technology has significantly smaller chances of accidents compared to old tech that was deployed in Fukushima/Chernobyl (boiling water reactors, whose design was built back in 1960s!).
Additionally I wouldn't be surprised if nuclear was much greener compared to wind/solar if you take a look at the whole supply chain and energy density that nuclear allows (I am speculating, don't have hard data on this). Hence I'm truly puzzled by the German energy politics (and even more given how reliant they were until recently on Russian gas).
One notable exception in Europe is France, where ~70% of electricity is produced in nuclear power plants! Huge respect for their government regarding this policy (at least in this regard, regarding their taxation system it's a different story :P).
I mostly post about AI here, but I also believe that if Europe falls back too much behind, it will be the end of the life style that Europeans came to love and enjoy that was built by the previous generations.
All of these things are symptomatic of the broader EU culture: anti-nuclear, anti-tech/progress (?), pro heavy tech regulations (EU is the inventor of cookie banners & GDPR while the development of actual tech is left to americans).

* How The World Really Works (Vaclav Smil)
* How Innovation Works (Matt Ridley)
Pragmatic Capitalism is a must-read. It helped me understand how the modern monetary system works (my old model was that of the fractional reserve system, old patch).
It also helped me correct some misconceptions I had, like the nature of "money printing" and how it really works (hint: in a credit-based system most of us live in it's all about private bank loans / deposits, and not Feds/central bank printing physical bank notes/coins).
Also helped me understand why USA's gov debt being 35 trillions is not actually that big of a deal assuming the money is spent efficiently and productively (my previous model was closer to that of a business/household which is obviously naive).
Angel & VC books helped me understand more about the world of angel investing & how the VCs operate, how they allocate funds, what are their incentives (carry/fee structure), who's their boss (LPs), etc.
The last 2 books are an amazing read and their title says it all.
--soft skills--
* Never Split The Difference (Chris Voss)
* What Every Body Is Saying: An Ex-FBI Agent's Guide to Speed-Reading People (Joe Navarro)
Helped me learn how to become a better negotiator and more cognizant of the body language. Both of the authors are former FBI agents with actual on-the-ground experience of these topics.
What both of these books have in common is that these skills obviously take a lot of practice in order to become your second nature. Nonetheless my space of unknown unknowns has been reduced. :))
--misc--
* 1984 (George Orwell) -> classic, I love "sci-fi"
* Design of Everyday Things (Don Norman)
* Meditations (Marcus Aurelius, Hays version) -> overrated :)
* Doing Good Better (William MacAskill) -> introduced effective altruism philosophy (loosely described as "the attempt to quantify good and maximize it") that is having a great, net negative impact (i'd argue) right now in the world of AI safety.
Its fork might be familiar to you under the name effective accelerationism (e/acc h/t @beffjezos), well there is also Nick Lander and accelerationism (but let's not go there ok? :')) Big part of the culture discussions in the AI space.
Now give me top 3 books that changed your life! :) What should I read next?

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
"To Code, or Not To Code? Exploring Impact of Code in Pre-training" new paper from @cohere. They explore the impact that code data has as part of the pre-training data mix.
Most of us have an intuitive understanding that code should help with reasoning capabilities and that that will likely translate to other tasks as well.
They did a systematic evaluation and their findings are that code is a critical bulding block for generalization even beyond coding tasks.
Compared to text only pretraining adding code results in:
* 8.2% increase in NL reasoning
* 4.2% increase in world knowledge
* 6.6% increase in generative win-rates
* 1200% increase in code performance
Obviously there is a sweet spot what percentage of your pre-training should consist of code. Going over that sweet spot will reduce world knowledge / NL reasoning, etc.
One caveat is that all these results were made for the 470M - 2.8B param range, so unclear how this translates to LLM regime (one could maybe call these "small language models") (?)
Check out the full paper here:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GVls4O4XAAAUl7M.jpg

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
OpenAI just released a new series of models that are more powerful reasoners! They do that by spending a variable amount of computation depending on the difficulty of the problem in contrast with your regular LLMs that always spend the same compute per token no matter how hard the problem is.
This is a step in the right direction as it is obvious that not all computations are equally hard.
They mentioned that the performance of o1 consistently improves with more reinforcement learning (train-time compute) and with more time spent thinking (test-time compute).
Note that the reasoning traces will not be available to folks outside of OpenAI, you only end up with the output tokens. They state that they do this for 2 reasons:
1) competitive advantage
2) so that model can be uncensored/unaligned in its traces
This is similar to humans' internal thought processes which we all like to keep private. :)
And also note that the compute per token (assuming they still use a transformer - which is highly likely :)) is actually the same but compute per "visible token" is now variable and dependent on the input problem.
The demos so far look really great:
* The models can count the number of "r"s in the word strawberry (usually LLMs struggle with this task due to inherent usage of subword tokenizers)
* The models can synthesize simple games after thinking about the input specification for a while
etc. etc.
Some impressive results reported in the blog post:
* "In a qualifying exam for the International Mathematics Olympiad (IMO), GPT-4o correctly solved only 13% of problems, while the reasoning model scored 83%."
* "Their coding abilities were evaluated in contests and reached the 89th percentile in Codeforces competitions"
AI is not stopping down :) we're combining algorithmic advancements with ever more efficient hardware. Things are just heating up, we'll have swarms of AI agents in the upcoming years.
Quoting @OpenAI
We're releasing a preview of OpenAI o1—a new series of AI models designed to spend more time thinking before they respond.
These models can reason through complex tasks and solve harder problems than previous models in science, coding, and math.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Lots of great insights from this amazing Physics of Language Models lecture! Let's start with scaling laws for knowledge. They show that "sufficiently" trained LMs can store 2 bits / param (bit as in information theory bit).
In practical terms that means that a 7B LLM should be able to store the information of the complete English wikipedia + textbook knowledge if sufficiently pretrained.
What is "sufficient"?
They show that roughly corresponds to the model being exposed ~1000 times to a snippet of information. This is what is needed to achieve 2 bits / param. With 100 exposure you only get 1 bit / param (they call this "rare knowledge").
Interestingly enough GPT-2 seems to be better at aquiring rare knowledge compared to Llama/Mistral (gated MLP seems to be the bottleneck) - gpt-2 is the GOAT! (long live llm.c :))
2 bits / param holds even for 8-bit (they mentioned int8) params!
---
Next up -> knowledge extraction. For an LM to be highly accurate at knowledge extraction you need either:
1) mixed pretraining dataset - i.e. both "raw text" (e.g. they used biography information) and instruction data format that contains knowledge extraction instructions (e.g. "What is the birth date of person X") need to be part of your pretraining dataset.
2) If you're doing the classic approach: pretraining followed by instruction tuning you really need multiple reformulations on at least a subset of your data (knowledge augmentation). By doing these reformulations the models learn better data representations (even earlier tokens contain the information that happens much further down the sentence).
An important point is that even if the model can perfectly memorize the knowledge that doesn't mean we can extract it succesfully. You need to use either approach 1) or 2) to get high accuracy at knowledge extraction.
---
Finally -> knowledge manipulation. By knowledge manipulation they mean operations like "Was person X born on an even month of the year?". They show this basically sucks without CoT, and even if you do CoT during training you still need it during inference (think OpenAI's recent O1 family of models).
They also show that inverse knowledge extraction is practically impossible unless you add it to the pretraining mix, i.e. teaching the model to answer "Person X was born on date Y" will not automatically allow you to get answers to questions of the format "Who was born on date Y".
This is also a way for you to discern an LLM from a human (i.e. there are types of questions where they don't pass the Turing test - yet).
Nice thing about this research is that it was done on 100M param LMs and the conclusions nicely extrapolated to SOTA LLMs. They also used synthetic data which made it easy to do controlled experiments.
────────

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] How does OpenAI's o1 exactly work? Here is a list of papers & summaries on LLM reasoning that I've recently read.
I'll split them into 2 categories:
1) prompt-based - enforce step by step reasoning & self-correcting flow purely using prompts
2) learning-based - bake in the above into the policy model's weights (or into a verifier - usually a PRM; process reward model)
--- Prompt-based
0) CoT et al:
Ground zero (plus I'm a C guy :P iykyk). It started with Chain-of-Thought paper. This class of methods boils down to asking the LLM nicely to reveal its internal thoughts (e.g. "Let's think step by step"; more generally telling the model to disclose the intermediate computation steps in someway).
A simple variation on CoT would be "CoT self-consistency" -> i.e. sample multiple CoT traces in parallel and use majority voting to find the "right" answer.
1) ToT (tree of thought):
Further complexifies the above (in CS terms we go from linear list -> tree): build up an m-ary tree of intermediate thoughts (thoughts = intermediate steps of CoT); at each thought/node:
a) run the “propose next thoughts” prompt (or just sample completions m times)
b) evaluate those thoughts (either independently or jointly)
c) keep the top m
cons: very expensive & slow
pro: works with off-the-shelf LLMs
2) Self-Reflection:
If incorrect response pass the self-reflection feedback back to an LLM before attempting to re-answer again;
As an input self-reflection gets a gold answer and is prompted to explain how it would now solve the problem. The results are redacted before passing back the feedback to avoid leaking the solution.
Even re-answering given only a binary feedback (“your previous answer was incorrect”) is significantly stronger than the baseline (no feedback, just sample a response once).
3) Self-Contrast:
a) create multiple solutions by evaluating diverse prompts derived from the original question (yields diverse perspectives on how to solve the problem
b) pairwise contrast the solutions
c) generate a todo checklist in order to revise the generations from a)
4) Think Before You Speak:
Introduces the CSIM method: 5 prompts that make the model better at dialogue applications.
5 prompts they use to help improve the communication skills are "empathy", "topic transition", "proactively asking questions", "concept guidance", "summarizing often".
Their LLM has 2 roles: thinking and speaking. The thinking role, or the “inner monologue” is occasionally triggered by the 5 prompts and is not displayed to the user but is instead used as the input for the user-facing speaking role.
I think these 5 bullet points nicely captures the main modes of prompt-based methods i've observed -> lmk if I missed an important one!
--- learning-based -> coming up in the follow-up post
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GZ7DjBAWQAASISN.jpg
────────
[2/2] One more here (I guess I should have classified this bucket as not a learning-based instead of prompt-based...anyhow :)):
Chain-of-Thought Reasoning w/o prompting:
Introduces CoT-decoding method showing that pre-trained LMs can reason w/o excplicit CoT prompting.
The idea is simple: sample top-k paths and compute the average difference between the probability of the 1st and 2nd most likely token along the answer’s token sequence. Take the path that maximizes this metric - that is likely the CoT path.
Has a good argument against the CoT self-consistency method: most of the solutions they sample are incorrect, only using their heuristic they pick the implicit CoT traces.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] How does OpenAI's o1 exactly work? Part 2. Here is a list of papers & summaries on LLM reasoning that I've recently read. All learning-based.
0) STaR: Self-Taught Reasoner
Ground Zero. Instead of always having to CoT prompt, bake that into the default model behavior. Given a dataset of (question, answer) pairs, manually curate a few CoT traces and use them as fewshot examples to generate (rationale, answer) tuples, given a question, for the rest of the dataset ("bootstrap reasoning"). SFT on (question, rationale, answer) triples. Do multiple iterations of this i.e. collect data retrain and keep sampling from that new policy (in practice I've observed people use ~3 iterations). Con: can only learn from correct triples.
1) V-STaR:
A variation on STaR. Collect both correct/incorrect samples. Incorrect ones can be used to train a verifier LLM via DPO. During inference additionally use the verifier to rank the generations.
---
[Recommended reading for 2) below]
Let’s Verify Step by Step:
They train a Process Supervision Reward Model PRM and show its advantage over Outcome Supervision RM - ORM (i.e. don't just pass a whole generation and ask for how good it is, pass in individual CoT elements instead; finer resolution).
Data collection: Humans were employed to annotate each line of step-by-step solutions (math problems) - expensive!! They've been given a curated list of samples that were automatically selected as “convincing wrong-answer” solutions - a form of hard sample mining.
---
2) Improve Mathematical Reasoning in LMs:
Proposes OmegaPRM - a process RM trained on data collected using MCTS (AlphaGo vibes? yes, paper comes from DeepMind). As a policy for collecting PRM data they used a SFT-ed Gemini Pro (instruct samples distilled from Gemini Ultra). Gemini Pro combined with OmegaPRM-weighted majority voting yielded nice improvements on math benchmarks. Suitable only when there is a golden answer, doesn’t work for open-ended tasks.
3) Learn Beyond The Answer:
Instead of increasing the number of samples in SFT dataset (STaR-like) they augment/extend the samples by appending a reflection to the existing (q,a) tuple. Reflection = alternative reasoning and follow-ups like analogy & abstraction). Complementary to STaR.
4) Quiet-STaR:
Uses RL (reinforce method) and picks rationales, which branch off of a thought, that increase the likelihood of the correct answer and subsequently trains on them. Adds new start/end of thinking tokens, and an MLP for mixing the rationale stream with the default stream. Interesting ideas, I feel that due to its complexity it won't survive Bitter Lesson's filter.
5) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute:
They first estimate the difficulty of a user query placing it into one out of 5 difficulty bins (i think they need 2048 samples for this!). Then depending on the query’s difficulty they deploy various techniques to estimate the optimal results.
They experimented with 2 categories of methods: search requires a PRM verifier) & revisions (afaik they only did intra-comparisons, i.e. they didn’t compare search vs revision).
For search they experimented with best-of-N-weighted, beam, and lookahead.
For easier Qs best-of-N is the best method, later it’s beam (lookahead never pays off). For revision they first do SFT on samples that consist out of 0-4 incorrect intermediate steps followed by the correct solution (to teach it to self-correct). Subsequently they test applying it sequentially vs in parallel. There exists an “optimal” ratio of sequential-to-parallel depending on the difficulty bin.
6) Agent Q:
Really the main idea is to use MCTS to do test-time search (according to the perf they get not according to paper authors).
The second core idea is to leverage successful & unsuccessful trajectories collected using a “guided MCTS” (guided by an LLM judge) to improve the base policy via DPO, this gives them the “Agent Q”. Agent Q + test-time MCTS yields the best results.
Note: they operate in a very specific environment - web and focus on a narrow task: booking a table.
7) Training LMs to Self-Correct via RL:
They introduce SCoRe, a multi-turn (multi=2) RL method. They show that STaR methods fail to improve in a multi-turn setup (due to behavior collapse as measured by the edit distance histogram; i.e. STaR models are reluctant to deviate significantly from their 1st solution).
Training proceeds in 2 stages:
1) train the base model to produce high reward responses at the 2nd attempt while forcing the model not to change its 1st attempt (via KL div)
2) jointly maximize reward of both attempts; in order to prevent a collapse to a non-self-correcting behavior they do reward shaping by adding an additional penalty that rewards the model if it achieves higher reward on the 2nd attempt and heavily penalizes the transitions from correct->incorrect.
---
That's a wrap for now, so how does o1 work?
No idea, but likely involves above ideas + a shit ton of compute & scale (data, params).
Let me know if I missed an important paper that's not an obvious interpolation of the above ideas (unless it's seminal despite that? :)).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GZ7SLALXYAAhpdw.jpg
────────

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Do we need language to think? The authors argue that language and thinking are two completely separate entities based on 2 main arguments:
1) They tested people with aphasia (language disorder) and demonstrated that their problem solving skills are unimpaired
2) Through brain imaging they show that the language areas do not necessarily "light up" during problem solving in humans
Some thoughts after reading the article.
First of all, I am very suspicious of argument 2) and would be curious to see the sample / group of humans they used for brain imaging. I suspect some people have much more developed inner monologues that are much more coupled to their thinking machinery. Toggling it off would likely reduce their problem-solving capability.
They also seem to treat LLMs as purely linguistic artifacts.
LLMs are not just linguistic machines, the "language" part of "LLMs" is actually quite misleading - they are really a powerful predictive machinery trained on next token prediction.
As a side quest LLMs do decode their internal representations into human language, but you are missing out on their whole internal world, and you ignore their training process, by saying that they are just a linguistic machinery.
My first order explanation of what language is, is it's a powerful decoding machinery of our internal thoughts, of our internal CoT / reasoning traces.
Obviously this is a simplified, thus necessarily inprecise model.
My 2nd order explanation would be that the language is certainly not a one way street, there is a bidirectional relationship here: thoughts influence language and language in turn modulates our thoughts (as I previously hinted, mentioning people with a strong coupling of internal monologue and problem solving machinery).
Maybe a useful (but not completely precise) analogy that would help explain what I mean by "decoding into language" is what o1 models are doing summarizing internal reasoning traces before exposing them to an end user.
But then again that's a 2nd order decoding, the first order lang decoding happens at the level of the autoregressive transformer (LLM) that is (likely) powering o1.
Finally animals also have language just much less developed. This is an evolutionary disadvantage as they can't share knowledge as easily (both with their peers and future generations), but it almost certainly also impacts their thinking / problem solving capabilities.
tl;dr I have a strong suspicion that this orthogonality that the authors claim is far from perfect.
>(jet-legged) brain dump of mine (flew from the valley back to Belgrade) :))

Some of my top learnings running startup(s) over the past year and a half:
1) You should be very comfortable failing publicly - especially when you're as public as I am about everything you do! :)
Luck plays a huge role in startups (timing, people, geo, idea, etc.), there is no way around trying stuff out, and most attempts are doomed to fail - learn from them! (and do so quickly)
One of my great character traits is: I really don't care whether people think something I did was a failure.
I'm not emotionally affected by it.
I love feedback so much (even from Reddit :P). The worst thing for me is a lack of feedback, and if I feel I'm losing passion/energy (scared to death from that).
2) My probably biggest career mistake so far was that I wasn't proactively working on finding my future co-founders while I was at big tech (but it's also quite hard to find people who are both entrepreneurial and great engineers, they're usually either or).
Keep a list of people you are considering for future co-founders, and nurture those relationships! Finding a great co-founder is hard! They need to match your pace, they need to be passionate, they need to be great.
3) Find yourself great mentors & angels. I was very lucky in this regard, I have plenty of mentors, whom I can call friends at this point, who've been helping me over the past year and a half.
E.g. @waikit is likely the most helpful angel/mentor I've ever encountered - I learned just a ton from him. @bobvanluijt as well, always responsive, always willing to help. Thank you guys!

They were willing to fund anything I do, they didn't care about the idea as much. They've been tracking my progress over the years and that was enough of a signal for them. It's really a priviliged position, and these are great people.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] New DeepMind paper: "A Little Help Goes a Long Way: Efficient LLM Training by Leveraging Small LMs”
They introduce SALT a 2-stage approach to pretraining LLMs:
1. Use a SLM (small LM) to bootstrap the LLM pre-training via knowledge distillation (the loss is crossentropy against teacher’s next token distribution and not against the ground truth next token one hot distribution).
Optional: use SLM to select the easy samples from the training dataset (additional form of curriculum learning). To compute the sequence difficulty score they find a median over the target token probabilities (with top-k filtering).
2. After N steps of stage 1 transition into the standard LLM pre-training stage (next token prediction).
They show how despite additional computation they achieve efficiency gains. Why? 3 reasons:
1. You only do a fwd pass through the SLM (bwd pass is more expensive)
2. SLM has less weights → less FLOPs needed, smaller mem bw required → faster
3. The number of steps before switching is usually in the single or low double digit percentage of the total number of steps
Similar to how speculative decoding uses draft models (SLMs) to achieve efficiency gains during inference here the authors use SLMs to make pretraining more efficient.
A nice parallel to how human learning works: in our early education days (elementary & high school) our teachers are akin to SLMs (less educated than university professors and hopefully our future selves).
Despite them not being world-class they stear most of us toward a decent set of mental models / representations / habits.
This is the KD stage of human life and indeed throughout a better part of this period of our lives we take our teachers’ opinions for granted, we memorize a lot.
Later in life we enter the self supervised stage.
For me this really kicked off in 2017, only 7 years ago.
Fun times ahead. :)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Ge6hQP1WgAAF-Yg.jpg

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Flying to USA 🇺🇸 - got some time to read DeepSeek v1 & v2 papers, here are the key takeaways:
First I'll just say that they're an incredibly cracked Chinese team - I'd put them somewhere between Mistral and OpenAI/DeepMind teams in terms of their prowess / capability to build powerful LLMs. They're mainly bottlenecked by compute (they apparently used nvidia H800s to train).
In v1:
* They recomputed the scaling laws from scratch (similar to Kaplan et al ("original scaling laws") & Hoffmann et al ("Chinchilla scaling laws")) - this gave them a framework to predict how to properly set the learning rate, batch size, data, params for a given compute budget.
* They concluded that Chinchilla scaling laws are not completely correct -> for higher quality data it seems you want to scale params more than data.
* They've put a significant effort into data cleaning stage: dedup across all 91 CC dumps (eliminates 4x more documents than doing it over one dump at a time).
* Achieved better results than comparably sized Llama 2!
In v2:
* They've done some really interesting modification of the transformer MoE architecture:
1) Implemented MLA (multi-head latent attention) outperforming MHA (standard transformer attn implementation).
Got significant inference efficiency gains (equivalent to only 2.25 groups in GQA) and allegedly better performance than MHA (why don't we see this in llamas yet? takes time i guess? or this is not reproduced by other groups?)
The core idea is to save a single low-dim vector that gets projected back into NH keys & value vectors (via 2 learnable param matrices) before doing the "standard" attention (they additionally had to tweak RoPE).
I'm a bit suspicious this works better than MHA, not sure i saw ablations on this (?)

[1/2] DeepSeek-V3 summary - world's most powerful open-source LLM:
--- Modeling details
* architecture: MoE, 671B, 37B activated for each token
* attention: MLA same as V2 (see my past summary linked below)
* multi-token prediction (MTP) training - primary objective is to improve training. Sequential chain vs parallel chain used in Gloeckle et al. They predict 2 tokens in practice
* MTP module can be removed during inference or can be used for speculative decoding for inference acceleration (1.8x higher TPS (tokens per second))
* auxiliary-loss-free strategy for load balancing - this minimizes adverse impact on model perf. Main idea: dynamic adjustment of the bias term for gating
--- Pre/post training details
* 14.8T tokens (more code/maths, multilingual beyond Eng/Chinese)
* PSM FIM (fill-in-middle) during pretraining
* 2 stage length extension: 4k->32K->128K (using YaRN)
* DeepSeek R1 synthetic data used -> increases accuracy (pro) but also avg generation length (con)

* 2048 NVIDIA H800 GPUs (compare that to @xai's 100k H100 cluster!!!)
* HAI-LLM framework built from ground up
* efficient training: 2.788M H800 GPU hours (includes only the official training run costs)

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
What is really Graph RAG? Inspired by "From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization" paper from Microsoft.
How do you combine (knowledge) graphs with retrieval augmented generation?
But first, few thoughts on RAG and my taxonomy.
RAG -> It really boils down to taking user's query, embedding it into a multidimensional (e.g. 768 dimensions) vector representation (through a pretrained embedding model) and subsequently using that vector to find the K most similar vectors (usually defined through cosine similarity) inside of a vector DB (using approximate search algorithms like HNSW).
Those vectors have associated objects with them (specified through vector DB's schema), and some of the properties of that object contain textual data ("the payload").
Thus you found K most similar text chunks and now you can feed them back into your LLM, and (hopefully) increase the quality of the response (or simply provide access to proprietary information that is only available to your company that the LLM otherwise wouldn't have access to).
That's what is commonly referred to as the "basic RAG".
Going beyond that we have "advanced RAG", I'll focus on:
1) HAR/HQR
2) Graph RAG
HAR - Hypothetical Answer Retrieval, commonly known as HyDE (HAR is an acronym I propose to match it with HQR) -> generate a potential (“hypothetical”) answer using an LLM (cost =1 additional LLM call) and subsequently embed the answer before similarity searching across your vector DB. The intent is obvious: try and increase the likelihood of the match.
HQR - Hypothetical Question Retrieval -> for every chunk, using an LLM, generate/propose multiple questions that one might ask about that chunk, and subsequently use those questions as "hooks" instead of the original chunk (when the hook is retrieved, by using object's metadata we can obtain the original chunk).
And finally, the “graph RAG” / “local to neighborhood”
This whole family of RAG is about creating a graph (graph = {linear list, tree, graph, ...}) around the original chunk and when the chunk is retrieved expand to its neighborhood. The hope is that the structure of the graph, and thus the neighborhood of the chunk is a useful signal.
This can be many things depending on the structure of the graph:
* child-parent relationship / sibling-sibling (e.g. we have a chapter and sections of a book and we use sections (child) as hooks and we return the associated chapter (parent) when we fetch those)
* BFS/DFS and retrieve similar nodes (i.e. the associated textual chunks) before fitting that into LLM context. E.g. if you asked a question "What is an MLP?" you might match with a chunk inside "Deep Learning" node, and then descending down a level you traverse through "Neural Network" node's neigborhood and fetch "CNN", "RNN", "transformer", "MLP", and other such nodes.
Microsoft’s "GraphRAG" is just one instance of the above, "graph RAG" is more general.

summary:
RL is all you need! 🍭🧠 Deepseek just released OpenAI O-1 competitor model (DeepSeek-R1 & DeepSeek-R1-Zero) with an MIT license -> tech summary
Their Zero model is just base model (DeepSeek-v3-base) + large scale RL without SFT! It achieves amazing reasoning capabilities. Note: RL = GRPO (not PPO).
BUT - they encountered some issues with it:
* poor readability
* language mixing (sounds like some cracked technical talent I knew that was poor at communication but great at problem solving)
DeepSeek-R1 is basically DeepSeek-R1-Zero + multi-stage training
This is how their multi-stage pipeline looks like:
1. Start with thousands of cold-start CoT data to fine-tune the base
2. RL stage similar to Zero
3. new SFT through rejection sampling data + supervised data (writing, self-cognition, etc.) -> ~600k data points
4. RL again - to make the model harmless/helpful, etc.
The length of the response increases during the training as an emergent property. Reflection, exploration of alternatives, and other approaches simply emerge without being programmed for.
Their RL mainly uses 2 rewards:
* accuracy rewards (e.g. unit tests for code can be used to compute accuracy)
* format rewards (gets rewarded if it separates the "thinking" and the "answer" parts by <think> tags, the reward that forces it to use the same language consistently without switching back & forth)
Interesating enough no outcome/process RMs were involved! So their pipeline is really simplified.
They also release 6 dense models (1.5B - 70B range) distilled from DeepSeek-R1 based on Qwen/Llama.
I definitely didn't expect Chinese to be leading in the open-source AI. Big congrats to DeepSeek team!

Few thoughts on the last few days.

It's LLMs+MCTS - same story as with AlphaGo/Zero!
It's tree of thought during inference! They're sampling multiple trajectories in a structured way and pruning as they flow!
It's PRMs! You need to reward every single line and solve the sparse reward problem!
Turns out it's none of that. Bitter lessons strike again [2].
It's "just" large-scale RL on top of a base model in formally verifiable domains.

(as I mentioned in my tech summary of DeepSeek R1 [3])
Simplicity + scale win!
Now shifting topics a bit - the markets, esp. NVDA (~-20%) have been down. I believe this is completely irrational, and likely additionally exacerbated by automatic triggers / machines doing trading for humans.

But that definitely doesn't mean we'll need less compute. :) There is no such thing as too much intelligence at this stage of our civilization.
It actually means quite the opposite [4].
Now that RL is back in the town compute will be needed across 3 axis:
1. Pretraining (10x-100x what we have over the next few years)

[1/2] so apparently a lot of influential tech/vc folks like @chamath, @naval, @snowmaker fell for this great but still misleading (i believe not intentionally) blog post by @doodlestein
the blog post is very detailed, forms a cohesive narrative, and is *mostly* correct (except for important bits at the very end that can completely skew your decision making)
non-AI experts like these guys have to outsource parts of their thinking (we all have to, on some subjects) to fill in the gaps in their understanding and i assume they picked up and propagated the misleading bits
-- here is what is wrong
the author starts by systematically describing various threat levels to nvidia's moat (my main counter arguments are at the very end, so if you want to skip to it go to "chapter 3"):
1. hardware level threat
a) companies such as Cerebras can chip away at nvda's training compute margins
b) companies such as Groq can chip away at nvda's inference compute margins
c) in general all companies are building their own ai chips
a) and b) is mostly reasonable, these companies do have *a* shot at getting a piece of the pie
the author then says:
"How should one think about the future of this business when literally every single one of these VIP customers is building their own custom chips specifically for AI training and inference?"
--> worth mentioning that c) is, i believe, mostly used as a negotiation tool for these cos to get better deals from nvda than them actually building a competitive ai chip (with possibly only exception being google's tpu chip)
author also says:
"When thinking about all this, you should keep one incredibly important thing in mind: Nvidia is largely an IP based company. They don't make their own chips. The true special sauce for making these incredible devices arguably comes more from TSMC..."
--> this argument is categorically misplaced, the manufacturing bit was never nvda's moat, and tsmc should be put in the "geopolitical threat" category, but then again it's a latent threat variable for pretty much all tech companies and i belive it's priced in (as much as black swans can be priced in :P)
2. software level threat

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Really cool (but also somewhat misleading) paper: LIMO: Less is More for Reasoning.
The authors show how they achieve 57.1% acc on AIME and 94.8% on MATH with **only 817** training samples.
The paper is informative because it demonstrates an existence proof: you can use only 817 "cognitive templates" i.e. highly curated samples to bump up numbers on some seriously hard math reasoning benchmarks.
I think it's not at all obvious/intuitive that this would be the case - this is, in my mind, the biggest contribution of the paper!
The misleading part stems from hiding all of the cost.
There is no mention of compute/human labor needed to get these 817 samples. So let's dig into that part a bit:
They first curate a large pool of candidate problems from NuminaMath-CoT, AIME, and MATH datasets - so far so good.
They then apply multi-stage filtering process:
"Beginning with an initial pool of tens of millions of problems, we first applied a baseline difficulty filter using Qwen2.5-Math-7BInstruct, eliminating problems that this model could solve correctly in a few attempts"
So here it becomes clear that the amount of compute they spent to curate their dataset is probably larger than just doing RL/SFT directly on a much larger dataset.
Both RL and their approach are ultimately just different search processes - so the really interesting question would be what's the perf/cost (where cost = {compute, human labor, etc.}) ?
Which of these 2 search processes is more efficient? (bitter lessons)
They had to run maybe 50M forward passes (assuming that they used k = 5 in their parallel sampling across 10M input samples).
And this is just the start.
"Subsequently, we subjected the remaining problems to a more rigorous evaluation using state-of-the-art reasoning models including R1, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen32B, and models from Huang et al., retaining only problems where even these most capable models achieved success rates below certain threshold through multiple sampling iterations".
They additionally used human experts to sift through the data.
And this is all just to generate questions, after this they spend a lot of time generating reasoning traces and answers and having humans further curate them.
For most people it'll likely be much cheaper, less complex, and faster (in terms of wall clock time) to just run RL and tradeoff compute for perf in a direct fashion.
Did you train on 1% of the data with 10% of the cost/compute or you trained on 1% of the data with 10x the cost/compute - in the former case i'm all ears but i suspect they fall in the latter category.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GjiIifsaIAQeNVW.png

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] How does GRPO - the RL algorithm behind DeepSeek's R1 models work? Let's dig into DeepSeek Math paper that introduced it.
Before R1 took the world by the storm, the DeepSeek team already had all of the ingredients in place: amazing engineering talent, sophisticated data collection pipelines and their new, more efficient, RL algo: GRPO.
DeepSeekMath achieved the impossible in early 2024: it reached Gemini Ultra's / GPT-4's performance on MATH.
The 2 main components were:
1) Building a high quality math corpus
2) GRPO
Their data collection loop looked like this:
* Start with a high quality math seed dataset (OpenWebMath)
* Train fasttext text classifier to recognize non-math from math text
* Go through deduped Common Crawl and recall a bigger dataset by sorting according to fasttext's scores (in the first iteration they collect top 40B tokens)
* Do a url discovery -> find which domains contain over 10% math data (as classified by fasttext) and add them to the seed dataset -> rinse & repeat
* After 4 iterations of the above they end up with 120B of high quality math tokens (they observe they've converged to 98% of the prev iteration's tokens being present so used that as a stop condition)
They subsequently do an ablation study and compare the quality of their corpus against Proof-Pile-2, OpenWebMath, etc.
The thing I didn't like here that is they compare against 50B (or smaller) datasets by repeating them multiple times. This likely puts them at a disadvantage. Instead they should have subsampled their own ds to the target ds size. This is a confounding variable in their ablation.
To train DeepSeekMath-Base 7B they take the DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B and train it on 500B tokens (56% DeepSeekMath, 10% arxiv, 20% GitHub, etc). This is the continued pretraining stage (next token prediction on web text).
This gives them a very strong baseline! E.g. it was much stronger than 540B PaLM-based math-finetuned Minerva from Google - although this is an old model so not exactly a fair comparison. Still impressive - a 7B model outperforming 540B model from a few years back!
For the SFT stage they collect 776K English/Chinese instruct samples. Questions were sourced from various maths domains of varying complexity and paired with CoT/PoT (program-of-thoughts) / tool-annotated traces.
This yielded DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B.
Finally they apply GRPO using 144k questions from GSM8K/MATH datasets.
GRPO works like this in practice on a single node:
* You spin up a vLLM server on e.g. cuda:7
* You pass in a batch of data to the other 7 GPUs
* "Micro-batches" are sent over to vLLM to do a single bulk inference pass (vLLM is optimized for high througput applications so it's a perfect fit)
* vLLM generates e.g. 8 chains for each prompt (this is the "group" part of GRPO)
* Sampled chains are scattered back to corresponding GPUs
* Fwd pass is done to compute logits and another fwd pass goes through a reference model (this is used to compute the KL term of the loss - keep the policy model close to the "reference" i.e. the original seed instruct model - DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B)
* All chains are rewarded using an ORM (outcome-based reward model)
* Now let's focus on a group of 8 chains that were sampled for the initial prompt: to compute the advantages in the group you compute mean/std of rewards in the group and then you do (r_i - mean) / std to get the individual chain's advantage
* Advantages are scattered across the chain i.e. they're the same for every token of a single chain (as we're not using process based reward hence all are equally awarded)
GRPO basicallly boils down on a high level to this objective: train a model that samples more of chains that have high advantage, less of those chains that have low/negative advantage and make sure you don't deviate a lot from the reference model.
And they achieve this w/o having to maintain a whole new set of weights on the device: the value model.
Subsequently in R1 paper they further simplified reward models and made them software 1.0 vs using LLMs.
They show that what their RL stage really does is sharpen the output distribution (i.e. makes it easier to elicit an existing knowledge from the model). This is likely a consequence of them using top-p sampling from vLLM and could be further improved through tree search methods, etc.
The way they show this is that pass@K does not improve after RL as you're increasing K, i.e. you have a less stochastic output distribution that can't be used to "search" during inference time. That's the tradeoff you're making with RL.
A bit heavier piece, hope you enjoyed it. ;)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GjmwYyZaIAAfzlo.png

[1/2] Surprising details about the Grok-3 release:
* Their current cluster already has 200k H100s/H200s. They initially reached out to datacenter facilities to ask how long for them to build them a 100k cluster and the timelines were 12-24 months, which was too slow, @elonmusk said they'd definitely lose if they went that route.
So they found an abandoned factory in Memphis, an empty shell, and built custom electrical / cooling systems, using portable generators, Tesla packs to smoothen out the power spikes (due to the fact they're using synchronous gradient updates), etc.
It took them ~122 days to build the whole thing e2e with 100k H100s. And additional ~90 days to add 100k more. No one has ever done something like this.
* Elon announced they're building a new ~1.2 GW cluster of GB200s/GB300s - this is OOM larger than any other datacenter in the world, and their current datacenter is already the largest single cluster in the world.
* @ibab said that while they were running Grok-3, AI engineers used to go to the cluster physically and plug off a node to make sure the run is robust to such pertrubations -> this is one of the things Elon does great, reduces barriers between designers/engineers, engineers/datacenter technicians, etc.
* Grok-3 is the first model to pass 1400 score on the arena :O
The scary obvious thing here is that due to the culture the team has, Elon's capability to attract capital and talent, and the rate of progress, I don't think anyone will be able to compete with them.
* They said they'll open-source Grok-2 as soon as Grok-3 is stable, in a few months. And they plan to keep that strategy going forward, open-sourcing last generation but still managing to stay competitive. They hide the chain of thought the same way OpenAI did.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
"Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space" <- really neat idea! We saw a similar pattern play out with diffusion models. Going from DALL-E to Stable Diffusion denoising was initially performed in the image space and subsequently in the latent space.
The latter approach won - at least with diffusion models.
What they propose in this paper is to directly feed the last hidden state of the transformer as an input to next sequence position, instead of first decoding into "language space" and then passing the token itself to next sequence position (which then first needs to be encoded using the embedding table).
The training happens in multiple stages - they first start with regular "language space" training (i.e. decoding every token and doing cross entropy on every single completion token).
Subsequently with each new stage they introduce `c` new latent tokens. The latent tokens are guarded by <bot> and <eot>. Before <bot> comes the question, and after <eot> comes the answer.
Latent tokens do not contribute to the loss, they're simply there to form a representation that is useful to the LLM and boosts its likelihood of successfully completing the problem using the following language space tokens.
The idea is very neat but there are many issues that need to be addressed:
1. Severe drop in training efficiency as you can't parallelize latent token generation and you have to run L+1 forward passes before you can do a single backward pass. As per bitter lessons this is a very unfavorable trait that, in order to be justified & adopted, will have to show immense promise in terms of benefits to reasoning/planning.
2. Lack of experiments at scale - they've only done small scale experiments with GPT-2 style transformer.
3. Lack of interpretability - adds an additional layer of opacity to already hard to interpret godlike artifacts. :)
4. The latent thoughts chain has to be constant - or alternatively - they need to additionally complicate the setup by training a binary classifier that adaptively decides when to stop the chain.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GrubgCPWsAEtsuG.png

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] New in-depth blog post - "Inside vLLM: Anatomy of a High-Throughput LLM Inference System". Probably the most in depth explanation of how LLM inference engines and vLLM in particular work!
Took me a while to get this level of understanding of the codebase and then to write up this one - i quickly realized i understimated the effort. 😅 It could have easily been a book/booklet (lol).
I covered:
* Basics of inference engine flow (input/output request processing, scheduling, paged attention, continuous batching)
* "Advanced" stuff: chunked prefill, prefix caching, guided decoding (grammar-constrained FSM), speculative decoding, disaggregated P/D

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] New in-depth blog post time: "Inside NVIDIA GPUs: Anatomy of high performance matmul kernels". If you want to deeply understand how one writes state of the art matmul kernels in CUDA read along.
(Remember matmul is the single most important operation that transformers execute both during training and inference. Most of NVIDIA compute is spent on it. Gaining 1% in efficiency translates to massive savings in the order of many nuclear reactors :P)
I, yet again, realized i underestimated the effort. 😅 Here is one more booklet (lol). 47 figures!
I covered:
* The fundamentals of the GPU architecture with an emphasis on the memory hierarchy, building mental models for GMEM, SMEM, and L1/L2, and then connecting them to the CUDA programming model. Along the way we also looked at the "speed of light," how it's bounded by power, with hardware reality leaking into our model.
* PTX/SASS, and how to steer the compiler into generating what we actually want (is that loop being unrolled, are we using vectorized loads like LDG.128, etc.). I've annotated one PTX/SASS example for a simple matmul kernel in excruciating detail. Even if you're new to compilers you should find this useful.
(i actually found various inefficiencies in both compilers - fun!)
* Many core concepts such as tile/wave quantization, occupancy, ILP (instruction-level parallelism), roofline model, etc. Also building intuition around fundamental equivalences: dot product as a sum of partial outer products, why square tiles are the right shape for high arithmetic intensity, etc.
* The warp tiling method - which is near SOTA assuming you can't use tensor cores, TMA, async mem instructions, and bf16. Just maximizing GPU's performance using nothing but CUDA cores, registers and shared memory.
* Finally, we step into Hopper (H100): TMA, swizzling, tensor cores and the wgmma instruction, async load/store pipelines, scheduling policies like Hilbert curves, clusters with TMA multicast, faster PTX barriers, and more.
As always lots of examples, lots of visuals. This is the first time i could see warp tiling kernel and be like "oh i get it completely". I just needed my mental image transformed into an actual image.
A few years ago I was really inspired by @Si_Boehm's excellent blog post on how matmul works, but I also found it had several errors, some unclear explanations, and it was quite outdated. Building on @pranjalssh amazing work (who did a great job building sota kernels for H100) and my own research, this is the final result.
---

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Attention is all you need and turns out we just needed even more attention in our lives -> Attention Residuals (AttnRes) great paper by the @Kimi_Moonshot team.
The name of the game is how much intelligence can you mine per FLOP per second per watt. It's all about efficiency and bending the slope(s) of the above relationship(s).
Paper shows that at 5.6 PFLOP/s-days (48B / 3B activated parameter Kimi Linear) Block AttnRes achieves a 1.692 loss vs the baseline's 1.714 -> equivalent to a 1.25x compute advantage.
(i.e. without this architectural advancement you'd spend 25% more compute to get to the same performance - a huge gain when you take into context the scale of modern AI clusters)
The main architectural idea is to replace the fixed residual accumulation with learned softmax attention over depth.
Typically in the classical transformer residual connections compress all prior information into a single state h_l at layer l (for each token).
Similarly to how in sequence modeling transformer improved upon RNNs by replacing recurrence with attention they now do the same thing for depth.
In their formulation queries are additional layer-specific learnable vectors, and keys/values are the output of the transformer block f_i (k_i = v_i = f_i(h_i)).
Due to various systems optimizations (e.g. they partition layers into N blocks and attend over block level instead of layer level representations) in terms of wall-clock time Block AttnRes only adds a negligible training overhead when pipeline parallelism is not enabled. Under PP, the measured e2e overhead is <4%. Inference cost is ~2%.
Now stack tens of these efficiency improvements year over year (across the stack) and you get something vastly more powerful than Moore's law.
Few interesting insights: AttnRes prefers / performs better with deeper transformers and it better regulates activations state / grad dynamics across depth.
Every now and then a paper comes out that you know will become a staple in our deep learning toolkit.

* Somewhat surprisingly (?) Opus 4.5 better than DSV4 Pro on complex, multi-turn prompts on Chinese writing
* Size of the models is still an order of magnitude behind frontier (O(10T) vs O(1T))
With 1.6T params (49B activated) OSS finally closed/crossed the gap (size-wise) with GPT-4 which finished training EOY '22 (!!)
* Agentic search consistently outperforms RAG - curious what this means for the future of vector db companies. codex/cc have already embraced this paradigm, and moved away from Cursor's RAG-based approach
* Ctx length extended to 1M
* Arch modifications yield 27% single-token inference FLOPs, 10% KV cache compared to DeepSeek V3.2!
* Pretrain ds size = 33T tokens
## Training (in)stability
They had loss spikes due to outliers in MoE layers (routing mechanism in particular).
2 hacky slns:
1. SwiGLU Clamping (linear between [-10,10], gate upper bound clipped at 10)
2. Anticipatory Routing mode - when loss spike is detected they roll back and push routing indices out of sync by delta_t steps; lots of optimization went in to get this working.
## Architecture:
* First two layers are HCA, after that CSA+HCA interleaved. These make it possible to go to 1M ctxlen.
* CSA (Compressed Sparse Attention): compress KV cache along seq dim (m=4 tokens replaced with 1 smaller-dim entry), followed by DSA (sparse-attn they prev. introduced). DSA does top-k (k=1024) key selection. Finally they do MQA (single key replicated accross all query heads).
* HCA (Heavily Compressed Attention) - similar to CSA except that m’ (128) >> m and global attn (MQA).
* mHC (manifold constrained hyper connections): more expressive residual connections. manifold == make sure that spectral norm of mapping matrix is bounded by 1 (transformation is non-expansive).
* MTP (multi-token prediction) + helps during inference with specexec.
* Additional branch of sliding window attn, because query in CSA/HCA can’t attend to keys/values from the same compressed block (otherwise we’d get non-causal transformer!) and local tokens matter a lot. so this adds an additional n_win uncompressed KV entries corresponding to recent n_win tokens.
* Attn Sinks (allows total attention scores not to be equal to 1, i.e. not a probability distribution anymore)
* MoE: 384 routed experts (6 active) + 1 shared. Surprisingly hash routing strategy for first 3 MoE layers? @suchenzang observed this as well
I’m also surprised they've chosen such a homogeneous attn layout, and didn't allocate more CSA layers to deeper layers (which tend to have longer receptive field). Likely for efficiency reasons, or lack of time for such ablations.
## Optimizer:
* Muon (@kellerjordan0 goat)
* They modified Newton-Shulz orthogonalization to 10 iterations, 8 using one set of a,b,c coefficients and then switching to (2,-1.5,0.95) stabilizing singular values at 1. I wonder whether this was in order to stabilize the training? People commonly use ~5 steps.
* No need for QK clipping (Kimi did this) as they do RMSNorm on queries and KV thus attn logits do not explode by design.
## MLSys:
* Wave-based EP (expert parallelism) scheme
* Batch-invariant kernels (non-deterministic accumulation order due to the use of atomic adds is avoided; remember that the floating point addition is non-associative so (a+b)+c != a+(b+c)). @cHHillee wrote nice blog post on this.
* fp4 QAT during post-training
* Efficient imp of Muon
* Hybrid cache management (compressed KVs handled differently compared to SWA)
## Misc
Focus on long context during pretraining, they introduce a curriculum: 4k-16k-64k-1M.
Curious why they didn't report HELMET, RULER LC numbers? Also I see a significant drop past 128k window, that's probably why.
Batch curiculum: start at small size and go up to 94.4M tokens.
Sparse attn introduced at 64k during pretraining.
## Post-training:
* Teachers go through specialized post-training pipelines (fine-tune + RL)
* 10+ teacher models distilled into a single student model (multi teacher on-policy distillation (logit-level not weight merging))
* for RL & evals they designed their own sandboxing platform DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec) in Rust - hundreds of thousands of concurrent sandbox instances per cluster

after injecting a piece of factual knowledge at step t=0, peak memorization occurs after a ~30 step delay (in this particular example, but the delay phenomenon seems more general)
the surprising bit (at least to me) is that only the batch at t=0 contains that snippet of factual knowledge whose recall is being measured. the subsequent 30 steps are injecting unrelated information
i would have expected a much sharper climb to the peak followed by a gradual decay toward a nonzero baseline
any good intuition? mechinterp folks?
the dynamics of charging a capacitor are the closest intuition I can come up with (with an important caveat that here the input is more like a Dirac delta impulse in current, in which case the capacitor would charge immediately - thus breaking down the analogy)
also relevant finding from the paper: injecting paraphrased versions of the same knowledge seems to reduce the slope of forgetting, strongest argument for why reprasing is a good idea mechanically

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
Thoughts on Kokotajlo et al.’s "AI 2040", a proposal for pacing AI progress (in particular their "plan A")
Some key assumptions required to make the plan work:
1. The US and China choose to cooperate on slowing down AI development, including declaring essentially all large datacenters / AI compute and allowing enough inspection that each side is confident the other is hiding <~1% of its compute.
2. All new AI training runs are temporarily paused, while existing models can still be used for inference. Datacenters are retrofitted with "inference-only" verification hardware so each side can verify, in a low-trust setting, that the other isn't secretly training new models.
3. "Total Research Transparency" is introduced -> nearly all frontier AI research (algorithms, code, prompts, documentation, experiment results...) is shared. Model weights, some training data, and other sensitive information remain protected.
4. Both sides accept something like "Mutually Assured Compute Destruction": new datacenters / AI compute are made vulnerable to the other side. In particular, their proposal is that US-owned datacenters are built in Mongolia and Chinese-owned datacenters are built in Canada. If one side chooses to defect, the compute can be destroyed.
Initial thoughts (incomplete/raw, given that there is simply too much to cover without spending significant time on a blog-format reply):
1. Obviously, a ton of effort and thought went into this, especially when you consider all the alternative branches they explore. I applaud them for putting it out for public scrutiny.
2. The cadence above looks like a chain of low-probability events. Re 1,2,3: coordination at this level between China and the US seems very unlikely (little historical precedent that something like this is possible?). Re 4: it assumes countries X (Mongolia) and Y (Canada) are willing to host strategically important datacenters while accepting the reality that those facilities could be bombed / destroyed if the agreement breaks down.
3. It doesn’t really consider what happens to the broader US (and thus global) economy under this policy, which currently assumes that revenues will follow the enormous capex investment that has already happened and is continuing to accelerate.
4. There’s a sentence like this in one of the plans: "Well, what happens next depends on who you ask, but answers range over possibilities such as 'take our jobs,' 'cement hegemony forever,' and 'get everyone killed.'"
The last few days of my TL have definitely felt like mode collapse around a narrative coming from a group of people who are, on average, much less optimistic about the future. I reject the above as the only 3 possible outcomes.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSDUvAlbgAAVpHj.jpg

summary:
[1/2] a few years after Kaplan et al. was published, while studying induction heads*, Anthropic's mechinterp team realized that the bump in Kaplan's scaling law plot was caused by the emergence of induction heads
(* an induction head is an attn head that does something like "[A][B] … [A] → [B]" i.e. when it encounters token A, it finds a previous occurence of A in the context window and copies the token that followed it. the more abstract the meanings of A and B become, the further we move from simple lexical copying and the closer we get to in-context learning)
it turns out that 1-layer transformers don't form induction heads, and therefore don't go through this particular phase transition, making their loss curve less steep
but with 2+ layers, induction heads can emerge

i haven’t completely thought this through, but it feels like once you have a copy operation, stable states (memory), and stochasticity, you already have the basic ingredients needed to kick off both evolution and intelligence revolution

summary:
[1/2] one of cooler findings (again burried in ant's mechinterp blogs) is that the double descent can be understood as a phase transition between memorizing individual examples and learning reusable structure from the data
in small-data regimes, models can memorize individual training examples by treating datapoints themselves as "features" and assigning them distinct directions in hidden space (the red polytopes in the bottommost row of the attached plot; the blue polytopes are weight features)
as dataset size grows, models transition from datapoint features -> generalizing features that recur across many examples (notice how the structure in the bottommost row gets destroyed, the model effectively undoes the initial memorization)
the messy transition between these strategies produces a double-descent bump in test loss
generalization seems to emerge once each underlying feature has appeared multiple times in different combinations (in the simplest experiments, roughly ~10 occurrences per feature)
repeated datapoints compete with reusable features for model capacity

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa) — thread (2 tweets)
clean_title: Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach
summary:
[1/2] looped transformer unlocks a new scaling dimension - recurrent depth; i think it received less love (other than the rumors that frontier ai labs use it) than it deserves, here are few notes / observations
fundamentally the method lets the model think deeper without increasing either its parameter count or its verbalized chain of thought length (the other 2 important scaling dimensions)
i find the constrast with moe interesting:
> looped transformer: keep params const, increase total FLOPs (more computation = reasoning)
> moe: keep FLOPs const (through active params), increase total params (more param capacity = memory/knowledge)
the architectural modification is straight forward, instead of:
L1 → L2 → … → L_n (where n = num layers)
we do:
P → R → R → … → R → C
where:
* P - prelude, few transformer layers that we apply only once at the beginning (i.e. L1 -> L2 -> ... -> L_p)
* R - recurring core, normally this would constitute the middle layers of the transformer, but in constrast with regular transformer R is repeated/looped an arbitrary number of times (r)
* C - postlude or "coda", similar to P just at the exit
so the computation proceeds as following:
1. e = P(x)
2. apply s_i = R(e, s_i-1) r times, where s0 ~ N(0, sigma^2 * I), and s and e are concat and mapped/"projected" back to hidden size
3. apply C on the final s (state)
(the particularly important design decision is that e is re-injected at every recurrence)
now the beautiful part is that more r at inference improves perf, and harder / more context-heavy problems benefit from more latent compute. e.g. on ARC-C they demonstrate:
* 0-shot -> perf saturates around 8-12 iterations
* 1-shot -> 20 iters
* few shot (25-50 examples) -> 32 iterations
(the recurrent reasoning is like a learned optimization in the latent space during inference; grad-descent during inference unlocked?)
--
the above generalization is downstream of how we train the model, r is sampled from heavy tailed log-normal-Poisson distribution during training
thus the model is trained across randomized recurrent depths (they use truncated BPTT - backprop through depth in this case - to save on memory)
--
few systems notes:
1. they synchronize one r per microbatch across workers, otherwise GPUs with small r would be idle waiting for workers that happened to sample large r
2. the model has a natural specdec capability -> draft model == low recurrence count (r), verifier model == high recurrence count. states computed during drafting can be reused when verifying! e.g. s0→s1→s2→s3 from draft (r=4) can be fed into verifier => s3→s4→…→s11 (r=12)
3. aggresive KV cache sharing is possible because every recurrent iteration uses the same weights, they show that caches from different recurrence depths can be aggressively reused zero-shot
4. latents converge quicker for "easier" tokens, early looping exit is thus possible per token, depending on how "hard" the token is
5. takes up less memory in training/inference (tnx to truncated BPTT and KV sharing respectively)
few mechinterp notes:
1. might be harder to do J-space/J-lens type of analysis (the deeper the model the harder it is to trust the jacobians that map intermediate activations to the output); in general this leads to more "neauralese" and makes it harder to solely use cot to monitor the models (i suspect that's what we've been seeing from oai/ant recently)
2. they find evidence for interesting structures in latent space, such as the tendency of the latent representation to follow "orbitals" to compute arithmetic tasks and for reasoning in general (the shape rotators win again?)
--
in general there is less need for long cot data, but it’s fully complementary one can and will do both in practice
another example you can do great work at academia!
soon we’ll have incredibly strong OSS models that can run locally, we’ve decoupled num of params from the perf of the model!
intelligence will be abundant, aligned to you, and democratized :)

[2/2] paper:
Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach
by @jonasgeiping @tomgoldsteincs et al, amazing work :)
clean_summary:
A looped transformer architecture introduces a new scaling dimension called recurrent depth, allowing models to think deeper without increasing parameters or chain-of-thought length. This method repeats the core layers multiple times during inference, improving performance on complex tasks as more recurrence is added, with saturation around 8-12 iterations for certain benchmarks.

Training involves sampling the recurrence depth from a heavy-tailed distribution and using truncated backpropagation through time to save memory. The architecture enables shared states and caches across different recurrence depths, making inference more efficient and adaptable. It also reveals interesting structures in the latent space, such as orbitals for reasoning and arithmetic.

This approach reduces the need for long chain-of-thought data and supports building powerful, open-source models that run locally, decoupling model size from performance, and democratizing AI capabilities.

title: Aleksa Gordić (水平问题) (@gordic_aleksa)
summary:
cool pretraining idea: token superposition training (TST)
during the initial stage of pretraining, instead of processing every token separately, group every s neighboring tokens and average their embeddings into a single latent token
that latent token predicts the next non-overlapping bag of s tokens
so for s=4:
[A B C D] -> mean embedding -> predict {E,F,G,H}
[E F G H] -> mean embedding -> predict {I,J,K,L}
(softmax target is 1/4 for the 4 target tokens in this case)
the transformer now processes ~4× fewer sequence positions, so for same FLOPs you can expose the model to much more raw text
--
big caveat is this assumes we're compute bound and not data bound which is precisely not the regime we're in right now! :') (but still a fun experiment!)
---
then switch back to standard next-token prediction for the remaining of pretraining (i.e. learn broad token co-occurrence/semantics cheaply first, then recover the exact ordering)
they demonstrate ~2.5× less compute to reach comparable/better loss on their 10B MoE experiment
intuition is that TST gives us a blurred, lower-resolution version of text first, then sharpens it with normal AR training (i'm sure one can make parallels with computer vision here @giffmana ? if nothing else Laplacian pyramid)
(cool work @NousResearch !)
